articles.title: Waze Now Alerts Drivers to Nearby Cyclists Using Garmin LiveTrack
articles.content: Waze and Garmin have announced the launch of real-time cycling alerts for drivers to help create a safer environment on the road. Going forward, when cyclists turn on Garmin LiveTrack on their Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin smartwatch, they can choose to show up in Waze as a real-time moving icon. Drivers will also see a notification when a cyclist is nearby, so they can slow down, stay aware, and share the road. The feature is completely opt-in, and Waze and Garmin say it is designed with privacy in mind. Drivers only see a temporary alert that a cyclist is nearby, and a cyclist's name, identity, or exact route is never shared in the app. Alerts also automatically turn off the moment a cyclist ends their ride on the Garmin device. Cycling alerts powered by Garmin LiveTrack are rolling out now globally to Waze on iOS and Android. articles.title: Google DeepMind melds humans and AI agents to vet Signal's secure messaging techniques
articles.content: Google DeepMind researchers have completed a formal verification of Signal's messaging security, marking what they claim is the first time AI has helped devise a proof that links protocol-level security guarantees to a widely used cryptographic implementation. They did so using AlphaProof Code, a multi-agent framework for formal software specification and verification. AlphaProof Code relies on a human-guided agent that writes a Lean specification, assesses machine code semantics, and crafts an agent-authored proof that the Lean kernel checks against the specification. In this instance, AlphaProof Code verified Signal’s post-quantum PQXDH handshake and Triple Ratchet , thereby validating the design of libsignal 's forward secrecy, authentication, post-compromise security, and handshake secrecy. In so doing, the Google/DeepMind team – Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger, Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, Charles Sutton, and Pushmeet Kohli – has taken a step toward a challenge the Beneficial AI Foundation issued in April to formally verify the Signal protocol and Signal app with Lean. The AlphaProof Code process involves working with various models to turn Signal's security goals into a human-reviewed mathematical specification. Based on this spec, the researchers assigned Gemini Carbon agents to generate Lean code proving the correctness of the libsignal implementation. After the agents generated 6.5 million lines of Lean code, they undertook an auditing pass and flagged bits that required human review. The result is theoretical in that it assumes perfect cryptography and doesn't guarantee the computational secrecy of bytes. But it's still a meaningful assertion of correctness. "It's a system that is fundamentally built for human AI collaboration," said Swarat Chaudhuri, research scientist at Google DeepMind and a professor at the University of Texas at Austin, in an interview with The Register . Traditionally, said Chaudhuri, you start proving theorems with well-defined problems formulated by a mathematician that get submitted to an AI agent for proof. In this case, the researchers had to figure out what to prove. "In formal methods, we always had this belief that verification is the hard bit," he said. "There's thirty or forty years of work on how to scale up verification. Now we are able to do that. So now the question is what are we verifying? … That process is fundamentally human-in-the-loop, but we devised a process of trying to scale it up to the extent possible with AI." As Chaudhuri and his colleagues note in their research paper, "AlphaProof Code: Verifying Signal’s Security at the Machine-Code Level," formal verification used to require heroic efforts. Formally verifying the seL4 microkernel took 20 person-years, while developing the verified CompCert C compiler took six years. AlphaProof Code, they believe, can drastically reduce the cost of formal verification, though their Signal work still took four weeks for a team of five people and "quite a few tokens." "The dream is definitely to scale this up," said Chaudhuri. "So you know there's been this rise in offensive AI capabilities, right? There are a lot of insecure systems around the world, and they're going to be exploited. "So what we really need to do is to apply this kind of technology to code at large all over the world and figure out what is it that you want to guard against? How do you write those properties, how do we specify those properties? That's going to be super important, but we have to figure that out." Pointing to a related DeepMind project, AlphaProof Nexus , which is focused on mathematics, Chaudhuri said the next step is to apply this technology during the software design process – not just to cryptographic protocols but code in general. "We really believe that the next frontier is not going to be proof but specification in this kind of research," he said. "And so that's why we took on this domain where…

articles.title: Steam Store adds average FPS data so you can see game performance before making a purchase
articles.content: Valve is adding framerate telemetry data to games so you can see what your hardware will manage in a given game before you buy it. The new initiative will start with the Steam Deck, but Valve has promised to bring the feature to more hardware in the future, presumably not only its Steam Machine but desktop gaming PCs more generally. The new feature shows players' average FPS on Steam Deck while playing the title, so customers can decide whether to invest without risking a purchase. Valve already added the option to insert your hardware specifications when you write a review for a game, but an extremely small fraction of players actually write reviews, and from looking at reviews on recent Steam games, it seems like an even smaller fraction actually select to include their hardware specifications, for whatever reason. This dialog is getting a new line to show the average frame rate of people on the same hardware as you. (Image credit: Valve) So this is a pretty interesting idea, not least because Valve is debuting it for the Steam Deck first. Notably, the framerate data Valve is using is sourced from users who opted into sharing this data, so there's no privacy concern here. It appears to be as simple as it sounds: Valve will capture your performance while playing a game on the Steam Deck, and then show that performance to other users—anonymously, of course. The clever among you may have realized "but wait, PC games have settings you can adjust, so even the same hardware might deliver really different performance levels." Correct! And it's also exactly why Valve is doing this. Its Steam Deck Verified program requires a certain level of performance, and games can get marked as "Unsupported" if they don't reach that level, but some people may find them playable regardless. In other words, there's no one perfect standard for "playable performance," and thus Valve wants to let users decide for themselves. However, this histogram is also available showing you the actual data that went into making that average score. (Image credit: Valve) Valve says that, at least for this early trial with Steam Deck data, that data is being filtered to only show data from Decks that are set to the default frame limit. The firm doesn't make any attempt to account for custom in-game settings, yet it says that "despite this, [Valve has] found that the framerate data consolidates around relatively narrow ranges," after accounting for the unusual effects of vertical sync. The library dialog that will pop up inviting users to opt in to sharing their game performance data. (Image credit: Valve Corporation) So what if you don't have a Steam Deck? Well, Valve says it sees this update (adding the Steam Deck framerate data) as "a stepping stone toward providing framerate data for more devices than just Steam Deck." Obviously, that includes Valve's own Steam Machine mini-desktop and Steam Frame VR headset , but presumably it will extend to folks on standard gaming PCs (whether desktop or laptop) It's not clear whether desktop performance data will be matched by graphics card, some combination of GPU and CPU, or multiple factors, but either way, there's no question that this is yet another feature that sets Steam as a storefront above its competitors . If you'd like to opt in, you'll have to join the Steam Client Beta for now; Valve says the feature is coming to all users "in the future," though.

articles.title: Bluetti launches an ultra-slim home battery to protect fridges from blackouts
articles.content: The Bluetti FridgePower keeps your food and temperature-sensitive medications cold for almost 22 hours in the event of a blackout Adding extra power packs can extend that to four days It's available now for £899 / $999 / AU$2,299 If, like us, you've been a bit baffled by governments around the world suddenly telling us to stock up on tinned food, radios and bottled water, you might be interested in Bluetti's new power pack specifically designed for fridges. With blackouts apparently expected everywhere at any time, the Bluetti FridgePower can keep your food and temperature-sensitive medications cold, even when the electricity goes out. The FridgePower is a super slim battery pack with an uninterruptible power supply that delivers up to 1,800W of continuous output, and a claimed 21.6 hours of fridge/freezer backup. If you want to keep your fridge running during a longer outage, you can add extra power packs to extend the protection to up to four days. If you think that sounds impressive, you're not alone — the device has just been named as an honoree in the CES Innovation Awards 2027 . (Image credit: Bluetti) Bluetti FridgePower: key features and pricing At 75mm thick, the FridgePower is designed to slide in beside your fridge or inside a cabinet, and it's wall-mountable too. It can send push notifications to your phone for peace of mind (notifying you of its charge level, and sending system alerts), and there will be an optional fridge-mounted display available early next year. Perhaps most interestingly of all, the FridgePower can monitor local weather conditions and initiate fast charging when a storm is forecast to make sure it's ready if a lightning strike takes out mains electricity. The standard capacity is 2,016Wh and you can add additional batteries to take that up to 8,064Wh. You won't notice it running either, as its noise output is just 30dB in Quiet Mode. This might be worth considering even if there isn't an impending apocalypse, because home batteries can help battle ever-increasing energy bills: if you have a tariff with lower rates off-peak you can charge the battery then and use it to deliver power during the more expensive peaks. Come the spring and you'd also be able to charge it via balcony solar panels or a portable solar power pack. The list price of the Bluetti FridgePower is £129.99, though it's currently discounted to £899 . In the US it's listed at $1,599, but Amazon is offering it for $999. It's AU$2,299 in Australia , down from AU$2,499.

articles.title: Here's your first Black Friday Kindle deal: get the Paperwhite Signature Edition for a record-low price
articles.content: Whether it's for yourself or as a gift for a loved one, a Kindle is a popular Black Friday purchase. And if you want to get a head start on your end-of-year shopping, then Amazon has just dropped an early offer on one of its premium ereaders. Right now, the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is down to £139.99 (was £229.99). • See all early Black Friday deals at Amazon This is a record-low price for the 2024 version of the ereader, which features a few useful upgrades over the standard Kindle Paperwhite, including double the storage at 32GB, wireless charging support, and an auto-adjusting front light that adapts the display to suit your environment so you have ideal reading conditions. Those improvements are in addition to the standard features found on the Paperwhite, such as a seven-inch glare-free display, a lengthy 12-week battery life, and a thin and light waterproof design. Amazon is clearly cutting the price of this model as a brand-new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition launches this month , with a new aluminium design, replaceable battery, and a higher contrast screen. Outside of that, though, all of the other key features are exactly the same. So, going for this older model is a smart budget buy as it's around £100 cheaper. Today's best Kindle deal With a new model on the way, the last-generation Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition falls to a record-low price on Amazon. Upgrades in the 2026 version are fairly minimal, mostly improving the design and offering a replaceable battery, so I'd be tempted to go for the older version while it's at a great budget price. You still get a bright and easy-to-read seven-inch glare-free display, an auto-adjusting front light, space for thousands of books, handy wireless charging support, and a thin, waterproof design. And it's all for around £100 less than the new model. View Deal We awarded this ereader a respectable four stars in our Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition review . We appreciated the improvements to the display and the extra storage space that enthusiastic readers will definitely find useful, while the faster interface and snappier navigation mean it's much easier to use overall as well. If you really want the most premium reading experience, then you'll probably want to hold off for a deal on the Kindle Colorsoft instead, but it's difficult to fault what you get in the Paperwhite Signature Edition while it's at this excellent sale price.

articles.title: Grab this GameSir Super Nova wireless controller at a record-low Amazon price, now under $40
articles.content: There's nothing that can improve the gaming experience on a PC more than a brand new controller, and this deal on a wireless gamepad is one you won't want to miss. For a limited time only, you can pick up GameSir's Super Nova wireless gaming controller for $39.99 . That's a record low from Amazon directly, and one that knocks 20% off its list price. ● Grab this deal at Amazon There are a lot of cheap controllers out there at this price point and lower, but they won't come with the specs that this GameSir controller has. For under $40, you're getting Hall Effect sticks and triggers, along with three different connectivity methods and a charging dock. It's also got an Xbox-style layout, although annoyingly, it isn't compatible with Xbox. It will work with your PC, however, along with smartphones, and even a Nintendo Switch. The GameSir Super Nova wireless controller is compatible for use with PC, Nintendo Switch, iOS, and Android devices. Its mix of Hall Effect thumbsticks and triggers means accurate control while eliminating stick-drift buildup. The Super Nova controller features subtle RGB lighting, swappable ABXY buttons, a detachable faceplate, a 1000mAh battery, and a charging dock. View Deal You won't be too surprised by the GameSir Super Nova's design, and it's a comfortable and familiar option for gamers, with rubberized grips on the handles and the Xbox button layout for the thumbsticks and buttons. It's instantly recognizable if you've used a recent Xbox controller, making it perfect for PC gaming. There are three different ways to connect the GameSir Super Nova to a device. You can use it wired, so you won't have to worry about battery life, or you can connect wirelessly using a 2.4 GHz dongle or via Bluetooth. The wired and wireless 2.4 GHz connections will ensure ultra-low latency with a 1,000Hz polling rate, which you'll want if you play competitive-style FPS games, for instance. Bluetooth will give you better battery life while using its 1,000 mAh battery. The combination also makes it easier to switch between using different devices, too. The GameSir Super Nova is fitted with Hall Effect switches for the controller's trigger buttons, and also uses Hall Effect thumbsticks. These magnetic switches reduce physical wear and tear, avoiding the stick-drift issues that have plagued plenty of older controllers. You've also got trigger stops you can engage for a hair-trigger feel, giving you faster response times in FPS games. There's also 6-axis gyroscopic movement that you can use in Nintendo Switch games, along with vibration motors in both handgrips for haptic feedback. It's possible to remove the magnetic faceplate and swap the ABXY button layout for your own preference, while vibration settings, button mapping, and dead zone adjustment can be made using GameSir's own app. The $39.99 sale price for this GameSir Super Nova game controller is a good one, and it's the lowest we've seen on Amazon before. Expect this deal to sell out fast, as there's no guarantee that this limited-time deal will stick around for very long.

articles.title: iPhone 20 Pro: Ten Big Changes That Could Redefine Apple's Flagship
articles.content: In 2017, Apple celebrated the iPhone's 10th birthday with the iPhone X, the biggest redesign in the product's history. For the device's 20th anniversary, all the rumors indicate that the company is preparing another landmark redesign. The commemorative "iPhone 20" model isn't expected until September 2027, but leaks have been piling up for months. According to Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman, Apple is already deep into its development , and the picture forming across multiple reports is of an iPhone that looks like a single, uninterrupted slab of glass. Here's what we're expecting: A quad-curved, all-glass design: The display glass reportedly curves away on all four sides, concealing the metal frame during normal use. Apple is said to be working with Samsung on an "equal-depth quad-curved" display to achieve the effect. Advanced OLED technology: Apple was reportedly planning a brighter, thinner Samsung OLED panel using Color Filter on Encapsulation (COE) for the anniversary iPhone, but a more recent report suggests the technology has slipped: UBI Research does not expect COE on Apple's Pro iPhones until 2029 , casting doubt on its inclusion in the 2027 model. Under-display Face ID and camera: Apple is reportedly continuing to test hardware that would eliminate the final visible cutout from the front of the device. Apple already debuted an under-display camera on the iPhone Duo's inner screen, but reviewers criticized its image quality . Whether an improved version will be ready for the iPhone 20's rumored fall 2027 launch remains uncertain . Solid-state buttons: Apple is said to be testing haptic replacements for the Side, Volume, Action, and Camera Control buttons. The buttons could be integrated directly into the device's frame, with no actual physical movement when pressed, yet retaining a tactile responsiveness. Apple modem in the United States: Apple is developing modems that it hopes will outperform Qualcomm's on speed and AI functionality; its third-generation modem, due in 2027, is the one expected to finally exceed Qualcomm's . The C1 and C1X are used in the iPhone 16e and iPhone Air, and the C2 now powers the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. Only the U.S. iPhone 18 Pro Max still uses a Qualcomm modem. Custom Apple image sensor: Apple is said to be developing its own stacked image sensor to replace the Sony sensors it has traditionally used for the iPhone. Apple has reportedly already developed a working prototype . The sensor is said to use LOFIC technology, which would let each pixel store varying amounts of light and potentially reach up to 20 stops of dynamic range. A 2-nanometer A21 chip: The 20th anniversary models are expected to feature a second-generation 2-nanometer chip. Following the A20 Pro in this year's iPhone 18 Pro models , the anniversary models would likely be powered by the A21 Pro. Silicon anode battery: Apple is reportedly exploring a new battery technology that uses a silicon anode capable of storing more lithium ions per gram, potentially delivering longer battery life without increasing the physical size of the battery. Mobile high bandwidth memory: Apple is rumored to be evaluating vertically stacked DRAM technology to improve memory bandwidth and boost on-device AI performance. Two sizes: The two anniversary models are expected to be slightly larger than the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, with Digital Chat Station claiming 6.41-inch and 6.96-inch displays , the larger of which would likely be marketed as a 7-inch panel. With all that said, we're still ahead of a rumored fall 2027 launch, and Apple's plans shift constantly behind closed doors, plus features this ambitious have a habit of slipping a year or two. Under-display Face ID in particular has been "two years away" for about five years now. Still, taken together, the leaks describe the most dramatic iPhone rethink since 2017. If even half of the features make it to the shipped device, the iPhone 20 should be worth holding out for. For…

articles.title: Samsung Galaxy S27 camera specs just leaked, and anyone hoping for major upgrades is going to be very disappointed
articles.content: The Samsung Galaxy S27 series is coming, and we've already started hearing a bunch of rumors about what the four upcoming phones might have to offer. The latest leak to appear online comes from SammyGuru , which features what is claimed to be camera specs for the entire S27 series. Sadly some of them are fairly disappointing. The Galaxy S27 and S27 Plus are tipped to come with the exact same cameras that we're used to. This means they'll have a 50MP main camera powered by either a Sony IMX955 or Samsung S5KGNG sensor — both of which are available on the Galaxy S26 series. The Ultrawide is expected to be the 12MP Sony IMX564, which has been in use since the Galaxy S2series. Resolution isn't specified for the selfie or telephoto cameras, only that they'll rely on a Samsung S5K3K1 with 3x optical zoom, and either the Samsung S5K3LU or Sony IMX874 for the front camera. Presumably, given what's happening with the other two lenses, we should expect a 10MP telephoto and 12MP selfie camera. (Image credit: Tom's Guide / John Velasco) As for the S27 Ultra and S27 Pro , we're looking at a 200MP main camera, with the same Samsung S5KHP6 sensor on both models. That isn't the same sensor as the S26 Ultra (the S5KHP2), so it'll be interesting to see how things actually change. The Ultrawide will once again retain the 50MP resolution, utilizing a Samsung S5KJN3 or Sony IMX855 sensor. Again that is the same on both phones, and the selfie camera follows that pattern with a shared Samsung S5K2P5 sensor offering 16MP resolution — a noticeable upgrade from the 12MP selfie camera on the S26 Ultra. The telephoto lens is where things change. The S27 Ultra will reportedly have a 5x optical zooming camera powered by Sony IMX855 or Samsung S5KJN3, though resolution isn't specified. The Pro, on the other hand, utilizes the 3x Samsung SK53LD camera. This is the same sensor used by the S26 Ultra's secondary telephoto lens, which suggests it will have 10MP resolution. So much for the rumors of a 50MP telephoto lens with 3.5x optical zoom. I figured that was too good to be true. Samsung's betting big on Pro and Ultra models (Image credit: Ice Universe) If these specs are to be believed, there isn't going to be much difference between the cameras on the Pro and Ultra models. While this has me worried that the Pro will inevitably start cannibalizing the market from the Ultra, it does make some sense for people who want a powerful phone that's a little more compact than the gargantuan 6.9-inch Ultra models. If a report from ETNews is to be believed, Samsung is going to be betting big on both phones. It's claimed that Samsung is setting aside 70% of its S27 production capacity for the Pro and Ultra models. That apparently translates to 18 million Galaxy S27 Ultras and between seven and eight million S27 Pros. The entire lineup will reportedly be around 35 million units, with the S27 and S27 Plus taking up the remaining nine to 10 million devices. As Android Authority notes, the Galaxy S26 Ultra accounted for around 50% of this year's production capacity with Samsung reportedly producing the same 18 million units. In other words, it looks like Samsung is hoping the Pro model will offer enough to entice people that would otherwise buy the two cheapest Galaxy S phones. (Image credit: Tom's Guide) The appeal of the Galaxy S27 Pro is that it offers more Ultra-style features for a lower price tag. Though to save on costs, some of those features will be cut. That's why the S27 Pro is expected to come with the 10MP telephoto lens, smaller 6.5-inch display and won't have a built-in S Pen. However, the popularity of the new phone is almost certainly going to depend on the price. With prices rising across the board, and a rumor that the S27 series could suffer another price hike, there may be more of an appetite for cheaper devices even if it means losing out on the ultra-premium features and hardware in the process. Then again, judging from the reaction to the Z Fold 8…

articles.title: 'Connected data is transforming the fight against fraud': New report warns AI is fuelling a major rise in insurance fraud
articles.content: Zurich analysis of insurance claims has found that AI is behind 20% of fake claims A complex pattern of seemingly unrelated false claims are believed to be coordinated by AI Generative AI has been employed by organized crime rings to create fake evidence for non-existent incidents AI has been driving a worrying rise insurance fraud, new analysis by insurance giant Zurich and AI analytics experts at Quantexa has claimed, with complex, organized crime rings have employed generative AI to make to fabricate supporting evidence in 1 in every 5 fake claims. Scams as diverse as crash for cash and serial claimants were intelligently analyzed with repeated elements flagged for investigation. AI’s use as both a generative tool for fakery and as a tool to detect patterns and highlight criminality demonstrates how the technology is taking criminality and detection into a new era. The analysis has so far led to £17.9 million in fake claims detected, a small number when compared to the £1.34 billion of fraudulent claims made in 2025. Fighting fraud Incredible volumes of fraudulent insurance claims have been detected over the past 12 months. Zurich UK found £109.3 million in total of faked claims, with £17.9 million of that identified using advanced analytics and AI. Some 4,359 fraudulent claims were uncovered, in motor, property, and casualty insurance portfolios. Claims identified as fraudulent increased 22% from 2022’s figure of 3,562 claims to 4,359 in the past 12 months. “Insurance fraud in the UK is becoming more sophisticated, more organized and increasingly technology-enabled," noted Scott Clayton, Head of Claims Fraud at Zurich UK and Chair of IFB. "Criminal networks are constantly adapting their tactics, whether that's staged accidents, ghost broking, fabricated claims or the use of AI-generated evidence. Explaining how AI has helped combat the £109.3 million of fraud uncovered in 2026, he added “Connected data is transforming the fight against fraud, helping us expose hidden relationships, identify organized networks and protect honest customers from footing the bill for criminal activity.” This appears to be an industry-leading combination of advanced analytics and human judgement by specialist investigators to tackle what is considered a rapidly evolving threat. Clayton says that Zurich is the first insurance company in the UK to unify data from “Companies House, Equifax, industry intelligence and the Insurance Fraud Register to give us a much richer picture across every claim. That helps us identify crucial connections and information that might otherwise be difficult to spot.”
articles.author: Christian Cawley

articles.title: Microsoft is giving Claude the keys to UK Copilot tenants by default
articles.content: Microsoft will enable access to Anthropic's Claude models by default for UK Copilot tenants next month, giving administrators a deadline to decide whether US-based processing fits their compliance requirements. From December 9, UK tenants whose administrators have not already chosen a setting will have Claude access enabled. Administrators can disable it, but leaving the setting untouched means opting in. In this instance, Anthropic operates as a Microsoft subprocessor , and Claude models are already on by default for most customers in the Windows giant's commercial cloud. The exceptions, notably, include the European Union, the European Free Trade Association, and the UK. However, UK tenants aren't in scope for Microsoft's EU Data Boundary - launched at the start of 2023 - and so Redmond is flipping the switch for the country. Anthropic processes the relevant data in the United States, Microsoft's documentation states . Administrators therefore have until December 9 to review whether that meets their organization's data-handling requirements and set access accordingly. Microsoft is also retiring the setting that restricts Claude access to Microsoft 365 alone. "This affirms Microsoft's commitment to offering choice between leading AI models while maintaining enterprise-grade security and compliance," the Redmond-based biz said. So long as you don't mind processing happening in the US. ®
articles.author: Richard Speed

articles.title: I love Ninja’s clever Belgian Waffle Maker, but it’s ruined my self-control
articles.content: For years, I’ve been envious of folks in the US as they’ve had access to a kitchen gadget I desperately wanted here in the UK. But the envy has turned to glee, as the Ninja Belgian Waffle Maker has finally made it to British shores, three long years after its US debut. What initially attracted me to this particular waffle maker was its apparent simplicity. Instead of the traditional horizontal pan, Ninja has given the humble waffle iron a 90 degree spin, standing it vertically with a spout at the top for you to pour batter in. Pour, select your shade level (one thorough five, depending on how dark you like your waffle), and wait. Waffles in an instant. It sounded almost too easy, and for $99.99 / £99.99, it’s not exactly going to break the bank — although it’s still on the pricier end of the waffle iron market. It’s no doubt an indulgent purchase. So I’ve finally managed to get my hands on it, and in the name of consumer research, have eaten an awful lot of waffles to determine whether the Ninja Belgian Waffle Maker can live up to my heady expectations. Spoiler - I can’t stop eating these damn waffles. So yeah, it’s pretty good. Stand up Another good thing about Ninja’s decision to go vertical is it saves on counter space. At 6.5 x 9.25 inches / 16.5 x 23.5cm, its footprint is small, allowing you to tuck it away in a corner or slide it into a cupboard when not in use. Plus, at 5.7lbs / 2.6kg, it’s easy to move and lift. It stands just 11.9 inches / 30.2cm high too, so it really isn’t taking up much space. Ninja includes a handy 'Inspiration Guide' in the box, with a few batter recipes, plus its Precision Pour Cup so you get the right amount of batter each time. If you find yourself needing another one of these cups, they’re currently available in the US for $17.99 (around £14). There's no word yet on whether we’ll get the same option to buy replacements in the UK. Future Future Future Future Future Future Future Whipping up my first batch of batter using Ninja’s classic recipe, and my mouth is already watering. I’ve got my M&Ms, freshly sliced bananas, nutella, cream and chocolate sauce at the ready. The guide suggests setting the shade dial to three (bang in the middle), which I think is a fair shout as it’ll help get a gauge on how toasted things get. I need to let the waffle maker warm up first - the red light will switch to green when it’s ready to add the batter. After around two minutes, the light changes and I get an audible beep signifying we’re ready to pour. I carefully tip some of the batter into the cup (the recipe reckons I’ve got enough for four to five waffles), and then pour it through the spout at the top of the iron. By what I can only assume is pure witchcraft, the batter doesn’t leak out the bottom. (Image credit: Future) Now I wait. I close my eyes, hoping for waffly goodness, as the batter sizzles away inside. After a little over four minutes the light changes again and I get the beep I’ve been so eager to hear. It’s waffle time. I press the release button on the side of the waffle maker and gently open the iron up to its horizontal position. Success! Sort of. I followed the instructions to use three quarters of a cup of batter initially. The result? Three quarters of a waffle. Wonderfully cooked, but I'm a hungry boy. We go again We go again, this time on level 4 as I'd like a touch more bite to my waffle, and a cup full to the brim with batter goes into the waffle maker when the preheat buzzer chimes. I wait, patiently, and I’m rewarded with perfection. I’ve got a whole waffle, with a little bit of excess where the batter has risen up the spout. I cut this off and snack on it while adding my toppings. The waffle itself is light and airy, and wonderfully cooked. Filling the waffle maker all the way and setting it to level four resulted in a thick, fluffy, perfectly cooked waffle Future Cooking on level five yielded a darker color and crisper texture, but personally I preferred level four Future It’s not…
articles.author: John McCann

articles.title: AI made coding faster. It didn’t make software simpler
articles.content: For years, the software industry operated under one core assumption: writing code was the primary bottleneck in software development. As a result, companies poured enormous resources into hiring developers, refining development processes, and building tools that could shorten the journey from idea to product. Then generative AI arrived. For the first time, the industry gained a technology capable of solving the very problem it had spent decades trying to overcome. The ability to write code – once the industry’s most constrained resource – is now faster, more accessible, and dramatically more efficient. But if our ability to generate code has increased so dramatically, why aren’t software organizations moving at the same pace? AI-enabled development offers a more nuanced story. AI coding agents can handle work that previously required additional engineering capacity, from creating the foundations of an application to generating tests and accelerating implementation. A group of two or three people can try out an idea that might once have required a much larger team, more specialized skills, and considerably more time. But speed is only part of the story. The more important change is that AI expands the ambition of each team. A 2025 study by researchers at Tilburg University found that while AI coding tools increase output, they also increase the burden on senior developers. After analyzing thousands of open-source projects, the researchers found that experienced developers spent significantly more time reviewing AI-generated code, while their own coding output declined by nearly 20%. In other words, AI accelerates code creation, but it does not eliminate the need for human expertise to govern, validate, and maintain that code over time. The implications extend well beyond senior developers. They force us to rethink what we actually measure. More code doesn’t mean more progress Excess code is only the symptom. The real challenge is keeping it under control. As codebases continue to grow, the question becomes even more pressing: if software can be built faster than ever before, why are organizations still struggling to move at the same pace? Because in enterprise software, writing code is only the beginning. Every change must go through quality assurance, security reviews, regulatory compliance, and complex integration processes. Those steps cannot be accelerated at the same pace as code generation. As AI speeds up development, what happens after the code is written becomes even more critical. Organizations are measured not by how much code they produce, but by their ability to run stable, secure, and maintainable systems over time. That is why the defining challenge of the coming years will not be a shortage of developers, but managing complexity at scale. AI changes the unit of innovation AI coding agents are a major reason for this shift. They allow smaller groups to take on work that previously required a larger roster, without narrowing the ambition or depth of what they attempt. That changes the unit of innovation. Progress is no longer determined only by how many people can be working on an idea. The implications extend beyond individual developers. As AI changes the role of software engineers, team leaders need to consider not simply how quickly teams can produce code, but how effectively they can define problems, validate results and apply human judgement. The real question is no longer how much software an organization can produce. It is how much of that software can be operated, maintained, and continuously evolved over time. What happens after the code is written The easier it becomes to generate code, the easier it becomes to generate complexity. Organizations can introduce new capabilities at unprecedented speed, but every additional component brings new requirements for testing, security, integration, monitoring , and long-term maintenance. AI shortens the path to writing software. It does not shorten the path to…

articles.title: EU's €212M border IT project lands IBM and Atos in legal water
articles.content: The European Union has dragged IBM, Atos, and Leonardo into court over years of delays to its troubled €212 million smart border system, which finally went live after missing a string of deadlines and leaving travelers stuck in airport queues. The lawsuit dates back to December 22, 2025, when eu-LISA, the agency behind the EU's fingerprint-and-facial-image border checks for non-EU travelers, filed its claim in an Estonian court. The lawsuit was buried in eu-LISA's 2025 financial accounts , published in July, with no mention of who was being sued. The Financial Times has since named the three companies after obtaining letters exchanged with the agency. In a statement to The Register , eu-LISA confirmed it had initiated proceedings "in line with the Agency’s responsibility to protect the EU’s financial interests." "The proceedings concern the system’s development phase and have no impact on its current operation. EES (entry exit system) is fully operational," the agency said, declining to discuss the ongoing case. The EES was supposed to be ready in 2022 yet wasn't live until October 2025 and was only fully operational from April. Travelers have since had to contend with hours-long airport queues and fingerprint scanners that reportedly struggle with sweaty fingers. Behind the scenes, things weren't going much better, with the consortium and eu-LISA spending years arguing over missed deadlines, financial penalties and who was to blame. IBM Belgium and Atos Belgium were already arguing over penalties back in October 2021, when they disputed a fine from eu-LISA and pointed to the COVID-19 pandemic and other factors beyond their control as reasons for the delays. By February 2022, the consortium was pushing back against another set of deadlines, warning that the agency's timetable was unrealistic. "Ignoring reality is not prudent and will not help to achieve the plan," the companies wrote, according to the FT. "On the contrary, working with an unrealistic plan will cause frustration for all stakeholders." The consortium also criticized eu-LISA's "overall governance," suggesting relations between the two sides had become rather frosty. The fallout wasn't cheap. The contract had already grown from €142 million to €212 million in 2021, and the delays kept adding to the bill. In its 2022 accounts [PDF], eu-LISA acknowledged difficulties with the consortium and warned of additional costs, with the setbacks also holding up other EU IT projects. By 2023, it had nearly doubled its annual EES budget to €40 million by diverting funds from elsewhere, partly to cover rising hardware and software maintenance costs. The FT also reported that IBM agreed in March 2022 to let eu-LISA withhold certain payments while the dispute over damages was resolved. The original contract expired last year, with a new consortium taking over implementation, although IBM, Atos, and Leonardo remained responsible until August. The project has attracted scrutiny for more than its ballooning budget. Last year, Atos reportedly used its Moscow office to procure software for the system, raising questions about Russian involvement in sensitive European border infrastructure. The EU's anti-fraud office, OLAF, found sufficient grounds for further investigation, according to an internal report seen by the FT. However, it referred the matter back to eu-LISA despite describing the agency's initial assessment as insufficient. Estonia's Harju County Court confirmed that the civil case had been filed, although no hearings have taken place or been scheduled. IBM and Atos did not respond to The Register 's questions. The EES may finally be up and running, but the argument over who should foot the bill for getting it there looks far from settled. ®

articles.title: Seagate resurrects hybrid storage: Hands-on with the FireCuda Forge – 8 or 20TB external hard drive requires you to bring your own NVMe SSD
articles.content: What's old is new again. Seagate started adding faster flash-based storage to its hard drives in 2010 , when solid-state storage was prohibitively expensive. And now that SSDs are stupid-expensive again (thanks, AI hyperscaler demand) the hard drive maker is offering up another hybrid drive, of sorts, with the Firecuda Forge. Available in 8TB and 20TB capacities, the Forge is an external hard drive that requires that you bring and install your own SSD. That's right, the drive won't work unless you partially disassemble and install your own M.2 2280 SSD, which mounts in the side of the enclosure. 1TB drives with DRAM are recommended. Performance maxes out at PCIe Gen3 drives; newer, faster, and roomier SSDs are supported, but won't improve performance. The Firecuda Forge only has a mounting point for 2280-length drives, and while drives that are less than 1TB are supported, that means less room for frequently used files, so "performance may be reduced." Interestingly, Seagate sent us a 2TB FireCuda 530R SSD to test with the Forge hard drive, which is both faster (PCIe 4.0) and more spacious than what the company says you should pair with its hard drive. The list of SSD that Seagate has officially qualified to work with the Firecuda Forge is also pretty sparse, including just three other drives: Samsung's 990 Pro, WD/Sandisk SN850X/GX Pro 850X, and the WD/SanDisk SN710/GX7100. (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) We only received a review sample a few days before launch, and haven't yet had a chance to put the FireCuda Forge through its paces for a full review. But I was impressed that, after I installed the SSD and plugged the drive in, it just showed up in Windows 11 as an 8TB drive. (The company says it also works with macOS 26 and later). There was no software setup involved, and Seagate says you can even remove and upgrade the hard drive to something roomier down the line. Seagate calls the "product architecture" that handles unifying and data handling between the spinning platter drive and the SSD "Alkemi," and says it combines "onboard processing" with the hard drive and the user-supplied SSD to "prioritize active data without requiring users to manually manage separate drives." Seagate says Alkemi observes workloads and gives priority to currently relevant or often-used data, that it adapts over time to user behavior, and describes it as an "on-device device dynamic caching and workload-aware data-prioritization technology." That sounds pretty similar to the SSD caching used on hybrid drives of the early 2010s, although with up to 1TB of fast SSD storage, you're getting a much bigger fast data pool than those drives of the past, which often made do with 4-16GB. Interestingly, Seagate says that machine learning is a part of what Alkemi does, but repeatedly points out in its review materials that it is not using generative AI. It's likely the company is worried about customers connecting the many reported instances of LLMs and agents deleting data with this new product. I can understand why Seagate would want to distance its hybrid storage tech from reports of catastrophic data deletion. What's the FireCuda Forge like to use? Getting past the somewhat odd-feeling aspect of having to crack open an external drive right out of the box and install another drive into it in order for it to work, the process was pretty painless. If you want to remove six more hex screws, you can also pop out the hard drive for future upgrades. But for now, we're just going to install an M.2 SSD. SSD installation is pretty much the same as putting one of these drives in any laptop or motherboard. Though you'll need a tool; the drive requires a a tiny screw and Seagate does not include a suitable Phillips head screwdriver. The drive bay is somewhat recessed, and…

articles.title: Lava Security’s Yakir Kadkoda on the AI Data Center Boom: Growth, Security, and the Risks in Between
articles.content: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence is driving demand for computing power, placing data centers at the center of a growing debate in the United States. While new facilities promise greater computing capacity, concerns over electricity costs, water consumption, and environmental impact have prompted calls for tighter oversight, including proposals to pause new construction . Beyond these concerns lies another challenge: securing the infrastructure that powers AI. As companies increasingly rent GPU capacity from specialized cloud providers known as neoclouds, questions arise about hardware security, shared infrastructure, and the isolation of customer workloads. Lava Security is a cybersecurity company focused on protecting neoclouds and AI data centers. Its platform provides visibility across computing, networking, storage, and hardware management systems, helping operators identify vulnerabilities, verify firmware integrity, and detect security gaps between tenants. We spoke with Yakir Kadkoda, Co-Founder and CTO of Lava Security, who previously served as Director of Security Research at Aqua Security and currently co-leads the OWASP Top 10 for Neocloud and AI Data Center Security Risks project. He discusses the debate over data center expansion, vulnerabilities in GPU cloud infrastructure, and the responsibilities of operators, customers, and policymakers. Q: Why does the U.S. need more AI data centers? What’s one example outside Big Tech where access to more computing power would make a tangible difference? A: AI is not a feature anymore, it is infrastructure, like power or roads. Every hospital, bank, university and manufacturer is going to run models, and most of them cannot buy GPUs by the thousand. They rent them. More data centers means more supply, lower prices and shorter waits for everyone who is not a hyperscaler. Three examples outside Big Tech. A hospital group running its own models on patient data: it cannot send that data to a public API, so it needs local or rented GPUs, and today it waits months or pays a premium. A university lab that queues for weeks on a shared cluster, where more capacity means faster science. A startup on a neocloud with no capex, living on rented GPUs, which feels every price hike first. Q: If Congress paused new data center construction and expansion, who would feel it first? Could the biggest tech companies rely on the capacity they already control while startups and researchers face higher prices or longer waits? A: Startups, researchers, and smaller companies would pay the price first. Big Tech already owns enormous compute capacity. Everyone else depends on renting it. Restricting new data centers would drive prices up, reduce availability, and concentrate even more power in the hands of the largest players. And AI development wouldn’t stop. It would simply move to countries that continue investing in infrastructure. Q: Lava analyzed publicly exposed data from more than 12,000 GPUs and found thousands reporting zero utilization. What can that snapshot tell us about how efficiently existing capacity is used, and what can’t it tell us? A: Between March and May 2026, our research identified more than 2,100 servers publicly exposing monitoring data from over 12,000 NVIDIA GPUs , representing roughly $100 million in hardware. Nearly 60% reported zero utilization when we observed them. That doesn’t mean 60% of GPUs are permanently idle. Some could have been between jobs, reserved, or undergoing maintenance. It’s a snapshot of a specific exposed population, not the entire industry. The bigger finding isn’t unused GPUs. It’s that thousands of expensive AI systems were leaking operational information to anyone on the internet. We need better visibility, security, and utilization of existing infrastructure alongside building more capacity. These are complementary goals, not competing ones. articles.title: Uber Is Launching Its Own Parking Reservation Service
articles.content: Uber is launching Uber Parking, integrating technology from its SpotHero acquisition to let users find and reserve parking garages and lots directly through the Uber app. "You can also filter your results based on criteria like whether you want to self-park or use a valet, or other specific amenities," adds Engadget. From the report: To book a spot, you'll need to provide the make and model of your car and a license plate number. Depending on your lot, Uber will then provide a QR code or you'll be able to enter the garage through license plate recognition. If you need to cancel, the company says the majority of parking options can be canceled for free up to the start time. Parking reservations can also be extended through the app. Uber One subscribers get 10 percent back in Uber credits on eligible reservations. When it announced its acquisition, Uber said SpotHero offered garages and lots across more than 400 cities in the US and Canada, but the company isn't offering all of them at launch. For now, Uber says Uber Parking will be available in Chicago, Nashville, San Francisco, Atlanta, Austin, Boston, Dallas, Denver, Los Angeles, Miami, New York City, Philadelphia, San Diego, Seattle and Washington DC. The company also plans to experiment with using lots as a staging area for the autonomous vehicle fleets offered byÂUber's self-driving partners. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: How to choose the best poinsettia in November for a perfect Christmas display
articles.content: Now that I’ve flipped my calendar to November, I’m counting down to Christmas and planning how I’ll decorate my home. However, I don’t stick to the usual festive tree and decorative lights; I always rely on seasonal houseplants to bring vibrant life into the mix. Apart from my Christmas cactus , a poinsettia is a must-have — it’s basically Christmas in a pot. Step into any garden center in mid-November, and you can’t miss a sea of crimson. Poinsettias have officially arrived and are the bright spark of color that signals the holiday season is near. But picking up a pot before Santa slides down the chimney comes with a risk. Choose the wrong plant now, and you could be left with a wilted stem by Christmas morning. So how do you choose the perfect poinsettia so it still looks good when Santa arrives in December? Here, David Denyer, flower expert at Eflorist , shares how to choose a poinsettia in November so it creates a perfect display right through to the New Year. What to look for when buying a poinsettia (Image credit: Shutterstock) Whether you’re picking a poinsettia for yourself or as a festive gift , Denyer advises checking the center of the colored leaves, known as bracts. “You’ll see small yellow-green buds, which are the true flowers. If these are still tight and unopened, your plant is fresh and will last much longer.” Did you know? The colored sections on a poinsettia look like flowers, but they’re bracts, often called modified leaves. The red ‘petals’ have developed to attract pollinators to the tiny flowers in the center. Bougainvilleas and passion flowers are two other plants with bracts that are easy to mistake for petals. Two warning signs that shout “don’t buy me” When you go to buy a poinsettia, Denyer says there are two red flags to watch for. He advises against buying a poinsettia with drooping, yellowing or missing leaves. It’s not a healthy start. There’s another danger sign to watch for before buying this festive plant. Denyer adds, “Don’t choose plants that have been displayed outside shops or near automatic doors,” and he adds, “they’ll most likely be damaged by the cold draughts already.” It appears that poinsettias prefer to be snug rather than chilly, so to keep your poinsettia protected, Denyer recommends, “Be sure to keep your poinsettias warm by wrapping them for the journey home; they really don’t like the cold.” How to make sure your poinsettia lasts through the festive season (Image credit: Shutterstock) Once you’ve picked a healthy poinsettia, it needs to be treated just right to keep it looking its best, which is why it helps to know that this plant is used to sunny climates. “Being native to Mexico, it makes sense that poinsettias love warmth and light, so placement is crucial,” says Denyer. “Select a bright room, ideally near a window where it can enjoy plenty of indirect light, but without its leaves touching the cold glass.” They thrive in temperatures between 59-70°F (15–21°C), but they don’t like sudden changes, so he says, keep them away from draughty doorways, radiators, fireplaces and open windows, as they’ll struggle otherwise. This attractive indoor watering can holds 35 oz of water and comes in sage green with a decorative wooden handle and a gooseneck spout. The durable stainless steel is leakproof, scratch resistant, and anti-corrosive. View Deal How long will a poinsettia hold it's color? According to Denyer a poinsettia will hold onto its color for at least six to eight weeks, so a plant brought in mid-November should see you through until the end of December. If you wait until December to buy your plant, it will keep going until the end of January. How to keep a poinsettia alive after Christmas (Image credit: Shutterstock) There are four main stages can help you keep a poinsettia alive beyond the festive season. articles.title: Midterm results will raise AI costs and compliance questions for IT leaders
articles.content: IT leaders need to quickly adapt IT strategies as AI and data centers will face more scrutiny following the US midterm elections, analysts said. Concerns around AI and data centers helped Democrats sweep the US House and Senate. Tighter restrictions, more oversight and slower approvals could slow AI deployment and raise costs. An exit poll conducted by SSRS and shared by NBC News showed that 56% of voters considered AI and data centers a major factor in their vote. The voter concerns revolve around AI data centers consuming electricity, water, and other resources, with the costs being passed on to consumers and local municipalities, said Jack Gold, principal analyst at J. Gold Associates. “There is not so much a backlash against the IT industry itself, but more against the thought that increased data centers will raise costs for normal consumers and do things to home values and land use,” Gold said. Over the next two years, there will be more pressure to show who benefits, who pays, and who answers when something goes wrong, said Stephanie Walter, practice leader for the AI stack at HyperFRAME Research. IT leaders should keep deploying AI where it improves the work, while building the evidence to defend those decisions, Walter said. “A new Congress will not fix poor data, unreliable answers, or an application nobody needs,” Walter said. “Do not assume AI services will always get cheaper just because technology usually does,” said David Linthicum, founder of Linthicum Research, in a LinkedIn post titled “The Midterms Put the AI Industry on Notice.” The election showed that AI isn’t just an enterprise issue anymore, but a kitchen table conversation. AI will face more resistance, scrutiny, and hearings, and “more demands to justify the resources it consumes,” Linthicum said. Building out AI infrastructure could get more expensive, and the costs will show up somewhere. “They may show up in token pricing. They may show up in enterprise contracts. They may show up in limited availability. They may show up in stricter usage policies,” Linthicum said. Enterprises will need to rethink how they build AI systems, Linthicum said. CIOs could adopt smaller models, use tokens more efficiently, and make more careful decisions about what runs in the public cloud, he said. Many Democrats campaigned on fighting AI, but AI companies and their capital spending have been keeping the economy afloat, said Anshel Sag, principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy. The industry waited too long to address public sentiment around data centers and AI, and could now be stuck with “spiteful legislation that makes it harder to remain a competitive economy,” Sag said. “I think right now CIOs need to think about their compute needs for the future, whether they have planned well enough, and whether they can continue to scale with the existing data centers and power they have today,” Sag said. There may be a shift in AI towards performance per watt, with total wattage making more of a difference, Sag said. Gartner analysts, in multiple research notes, advised companies to “reassess AI business cases under increased compute-cost and reduced infrastructure-availability scenarios.” US President Donald Trump, a Republican, has been hands-off with AI regulation. He has said he is willing to work with the Democrats in passing legislation but has also expressed his willingness to veto legislation. “A Democratic majority in the US House and Senate and a Republican presidency will likely result in legislative gridlock as the president uses his veto power,” the Gartner analysts wrote. Federal inaction could result in states taking action in areas such as AI governance, data center development, energy infrastructure, and environmental regulation, the analysts wrote. AI vendors should “be prepared for increased requests for disclosure of testing, safety controls, privacy practices, data provenance, bias management methods, human oversight, and procurement justifications,”…

articles.title: The weird and brilliant innovations that led to electroconvulsive therapy—and the mystery of why it works
articles.content: When I began considering electroconvulsive therapy, better known as electroshock, I assumed the “shock” part referred to the electrical zap you received. An electrode or two on your head. Some doctor pressing a button. A machine buzzed audibly. Zap, zap . You were shocked. Maybe changed forever. Maybe for good, maybe for ill. Zap, zap . Like a ray gun in a dystopian thriller. And no thriller was more dystopian (I flattered myself) than the anxious depression that had me in agony every waking moment. Before I met those electrodes, accepted them onto my temples and into my life, my doctors gave me some books to read. I learned that most of what I thought I knew about ECT was deeply wrong. The real story was both grislier and more hopeful than you probably know. THE FIRST SHOCK TREATMENTS: FEVERS, INSULIN, AND ELECTROCUTED PIGS When the Romanian-born psychiatrist Constance Pascal began using the term “shock” ( choc ) in her psychiatric clinic in France, around 1926, she was referring to physical treatments meant to surprise or disturb the body and brain, restoring the mind to equilibrium. Pascal considered mental illnesses to be a kind of allergic reaction, and she argued that resetting the brain and nervous system would be necessary for recovery. Pascal’s first shock therapies, in the late 1920s, used various means to prompt a reset, including induced fevers. Around the same time, in 1927 Berlin, the neurophysiologist Manfred Sakel was developing a new form of shock treatment in which a patient received potent injections of insulin. At proper doses, Sakel found he could induce a grand mal seizure as the patient came out of a hypoglycemic coma. Insulin coma therapy produced astonishingly positive results for mood disorders—sometimes. (One famous recipient was the storied mathematician John Nash, who received insulin shocks for schizophrenia in 1961.) But results were markedly uneven. Ladislas Meduna, the Hungarian neuropathologist, shared Pascal’s interest in the possibilities of shock therapies and came to wonder whether seizures might offer a better route to healing. In autopsies of epileptics, Meduna observed that the brains showed “tremendous changes” that were “just the opposite of those found in schizophrenia” (then a broad term that could encompass depression, schizoaffective disorders, and much more). In particular, Meduna noted that the glia—supportive cells sometimes called the janitors of the brain, whose duties include tending to our neurons—were overproduced in the brain tissue of epileptics, and vastly underrepresented in the cranial autopsies of patients with advanced mood disorders. Pursuing this apparent antagonism between seizures and psychosis, Meduna introduced a new shock therapy in late 1934, injecting a catatonic patient with camphor, the compound then used in mothballs. Three weeks and five camphor-assisted seizures later, the patient was moving and talking—two things he hadn’t done in four years. Meduna repeated this apparent success with four subsequent patients, sometimes replacing camphor with the synthetic compound pentylenetetrazol, branded as Metrazol or Cardiazol, which achieved a similar convulsion but faster. It was also safer than insulin comas, which carried a real risk of death. Still, Metrazol had severe drawbacks. One of the biggest was that the chemical seemed to induce feelings of absolute terror in patients before they finally fell into the coma. Not ideal for subjects already managing profound mental disturbances. Meanwhile, in Italy, they were beginning to practice a new form of shocking the system, one that worked faster and more effectively than insulin or Metrazol—even if no one quite knew how it worked in the first place. At the Clinic for Nervous and Mental Disorders in Rome, a little after 11 a.m. on April 11, 1938, the neurologist Ugo Cerletti placed a pair of electrodes on the temples of a man identified as “Enrico X.” Cerletti and his colleague, Lucio Bini, used a rubber band…

articles.title: Anyone Can Copy Your Crypto App. Can They Copy Your Business?
articles.content: For much of his career, Aleksei Voiutskii has been working on a problem that technology founders often underestimate: how to turn a product into a viable business. He founded NODES as a marketing consultancy, later expanded its work into technology solutions, and now evaluates emerging companies from another perspective – as a private investor and business angel. Through NODES’ Startup Accelerator and Crypto Advisory practices, he also helps technology founders navigate the journey from product development to market entry and scale. That combination of experience in marketing, user acquisition, technology, and investing gives Voiutskii a particular perspective on one of the questions facing Web3 today: what happens to a startup when the technology behind its product becomes easy to replicate? “When I evaluate a startup, the number of impressive features it has is not what interests me most,” Voiutskii says. “I want to understand why customers would choose this particular business, trust it with their money, and keep using its product even if a competitor offered almost identical technology.” For Web3, that question is becoming harder to ignore. AI-powered development tools are lowering the barrier to entry. Open APIs provide access to sophisticated trading infrastructure. Features that once required substantial engineering resources can now be reproduced in a fraction of the time. But as building a crypto application becomes easier, convincing users to trust it becomes a much more difficult proposition. Security Isn't a New Problem. The Competitive Landscape Is. Security has been a fundamental concern in crypto since the industry's earliest days. Over the years, companies have significantly improved the technologies used to protect digital assets. But as financial infrastructure becomes more sophisticated, risk management grows more complicated. Today, the security of a trading platform depends on far more than the underlying blockchain or its smart contracts. Third-party providers, internal systems, authentication mechanisms, and operational procedures all contribute to the platform's overall resilience. Recent incidents involving major crypto platforms illustrate just how much this broader infrastructure matters. On October 29, Polymarket reported a security incident involving a third-party technology provider. The incident did not involve a vulnerability in Polymarket’s smart contracts, which continued to function as intended. As a precaution, the company temporarily suspended trading, addressed the issue, and restored platform operations. Polymarket also said it would fully compensate affected users for their losses. On October 30, Binance published preliminary findings from a separate security investigation. The exchange outlined measures taken to contain the incident, including temporarily suspending deposits and withdrawals for additional checks and freezing some affected funds. Binance also stated that it had found no evidence that wallet private keys had been compromised and said it intended to cover users' losses. The incidents differed in both their causes and circumstances. But they illustrate a common reality of running a financial platform: security is not simply about preventing something from going wrong. It is also about responding effectively when something does go wrong, protecting customers, and keeping the business operational. None of this is new to Web3. What is changing is the competitive environment in which these responsibilities must be fulfilled. Users now have access to a growing number of products built on increasingly similar technological foundations. As functionality becomes easier to reproduce, reliability, security, and user experience become more important ways for companies to differentiate themselves. And trust is not built through security architecture alone. It also depends on whether a company consistently delivers on its promises to customers. When Crypto Startups Start Thinking Like…

articles.title: All net-connected vehicles from two major automakers allowed hackers to remotely unlock doors and start the engine
articles.content: Before proceeding further, we'd like to advise our dear reader to sit down and perhaps grab a helmet, for this post will elicit quite a few face-palms and forehead-slaps. Two security researchers joined forces and, during early 2026, managed to hack the vehicle connectivity backend infrastructure of two automakers , managing to remotely open the doors on any of their net-connected cars and start their engines across multiple world regions. The vulnerabilities were quickly fixed, and they pertained to a handful of belief-begging security issues with multiple server APIs that their respective mobile applications use. Furthermore, although remotely opening the cars and starting them were the most concerning bits, the vulnerabilities also exposed the vehicles' location, mileage, fuel, range, door states, and the customers' personal information. The white-hat hacking duo isn't disclosing the name of the impacted automakers, but they managed to get access to Automaker #1's U.S. vehicles, while vehicles from Automaker #2 were susceptible to unplanned lock disengagement in Australia, the U.S., and Canada. As far as we can tell by visual inspection alone, the second firm may be Toyota, as the hack demonstration video appears to depict a RAV4 SUV. Both affected automakers use ForgeRock's authentication and authorization services, though with the one small exception, the vulnerabilities found by Shubham Shah and Sam Curry pertained to poor implementations and security practices. One of their writeups goes over the ForgeRock-related affairs in detail for both companies, while Shah's article discusses the specifics on automaker #2 and their Australian connected-car infrastructure. Shah first decompiled the company's Android application and found network calls to a telematics subdomain, quickly finding an "admintool" location containing a "TEST HARNESS" page with a login prompt. If you haven't been keeping track by now, the first problem is that this endpoint is reachable from the internet at large. But what really piqued Shah's interest was problem #2: a bundle of JavaScript code that should have been stripped of any unnecessary cruft actually contained the code for the backend's entire functionality, providing a map for further shenanigans. This alone was enough to grant Shah the ability to pull up customer information with API keys that were hard-coded into said JavaScript. After some careful chaining of requests and connecting a license plate to a VIN with publicly available info, he connected that to a customer and found their email. At this point, the team noticed that the automaker was using ForgeRock's authentication mechanisms, and spent "a couple weeks" finding how they were used. And this is also where they assess that the easiest path to victory is managing to mint an access token for any user, a task made way easier by the "cursed" JavaScript bundle they found at an endpoint containing hard-coded administrator credentials . These were likely meant for the staging environment, but the duo estimated, correctly, that they could be leveraged nevertheless. At this point, they ran into the WAF in front of the service. A Web Application Firewall is similar to a network firewall, but instead of working with IPs and ports, it considers endpoints (URLs) and the requirements to access them. The researchers hypothesize that although it's a good and standard practice, the WAF was put in place because of how bad things were underneath. And they were right. The app decompilation had revealed a "pinService", and Shah found that it was accessible through the WAF. From thereon, they found "getUser", and correctly guessed that they could retrieve users' information with their email, phone, and ID. Remember those admin credentials? They came in handy, revealing the users' password hashes, but as these were SHA-512, cracking them was unfeasible. At this point, they let GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra loose to brute-force path names, and found an unprotected one…

articles.title: Netflix top 10 shows — here’s the 3 you need to binge-watch this week (November 10-16)
articles.content: Netflix's top 10 shows list is always changing, which can make it tricky to know what’s actually worth adding to your watchlist. With new releases arriving every week and hit shows climbing back up the rankings, there’s usually plenty to choose from. But if you’re anything like me, you don’t always have time to sift through dozens of titles to find your next binge-watch. So, I’ve taken a look at what’s currently trending on Netflix and picked out three shows that deserve your attention this week. Whether you’re after a twist-filled spy thriller about a secret agent, a warm-hearted comedy set in a small Arctic community, or a gripping prison drama, there’s something here for you. These are the three Netflix top 10 shows I’d put at the top of my watchlist right now. Note: This list is based on the Netflix U.S. top 10 shows as of Tuesday, November 10, 2026. Best shows in the Netflix top 10 ‘Black Doves’ The second season of “Black Doves” is here, which means you have six new episodes to binge-watch this week. Originally planned as a limited series, the spy thriller proved popular enough to earn a second outing, with creator Joe Barton and production company Sister returning for another chapter. I’d also argue it deserves a place among this year’s Christmas viewing, thanks to its wintry London backdrop, complete with sparkling festive displays and freezing streets. The story itself is far from cozy, but that contrast makes it an interesting choice for the holiday season. Helen Webb (Keira Knightley) leads a double life as an undercover spy for a secretive organization that sells stolen intelligence to the highest bidder. When her secret lover is murdered, Helen teams up with her longtime friend Sam (Ben Whishaw), a professional hitman, to investigate his death. Season 2 sees Helen continue passing government secrets to the Black Doves as her husband Wallace prepares to become prime minister. When her handler, Mrs. Reed (Sarah Lancashire), becomes caught up in a plot to undermine her position, Helen reunites with Sam. Stream "Black Doves" season 2 on Netflix ‘North of North’ “North of North” is also back for season 2, giving fans another chance to spend time with its quirky Arctic community. The comedy-drama made history as Netflix’s first Canadian original series produced directly in Nunavut, and its distinctive setting is a big part of what makes it stand out. Director Anya Adams, whose credits include “Yellowjackets” and “Abbott Elementary,” helps bring plenty of personality to the ensemble. With the show already making an appearance in Netflix’s top 10, there’s plenty of reason to give this one a try. Siaja (Anna Lambe) is a young Inuk mother who makes a very public exit from her marriage and attempts to start afresh with her young daughter in the small Arctic town of Ice Cove, Nunavut. Between finding a job and adjusting to single parenthood, she quickly discovers that rebuilding her life won’t be straightforward. In season 2, Siaja is determined to take on more responsibility at the community center while getting to know a half-sister she never knew existed. Newly divorced, she’s also open to dating again, all while raising Bun. Stream "North of North" season 2 on Netflix ‘Rectify’ “Rectify” is a critically acclaimed Southern Gothic drama that deserves more attention from fans of character-driven TV. The series was the first fully owned original scripted drama developed for SundanceTV and ran for four seasons, with 30 episodes in total. Its slower pace and cinematic approach give the story room to explore its characters in a way that feels closer to independent filmmaking than traditional cable drama. The show also received a Peabody Award in 2014, securing it as one of the standout dramas of its era. Daniel Holden (Aden Young) is released from death row after spending 19 years in prison for the alleged murder of his teenage girlfriend. New DNA evidence overturns his conviction, allowing him to return to his childhood home…

articles.title: A GUI Agent Hits 79.5% on OSWorld by Training on Real-World Device Tasks
articles.content: Qwen-UI-Agent Technical Report: Toward Next-Generation Real-World Centric Foundation GUI Agents Authors: Hanzhang Zhou, Panrong Tong, Xu Zhang, Quyu Kong, Chenglin Cai, Tianyu Xia, Gongjie Zhang, Jianan Zhang, Long Li, Long Chen, Lei Wang, Gaole Dai, Pengxiang Li, Liangyu Chen, Yue Wang, Steven Hoi (Alibaba Tongyi Lab) Editor's note: HackerNoon is republishing this paper in full for the record, with credit to all of its authors. It was originally published on arXiv as arXiv:2607.28227 under a CC BY 4.0 license . The original title appears above. HackerNoon added a new headline and adapted the formatting from arXiv's HTML version. The paper's text, figures, tables and references are otherwise unchanged. Abstract GUI agents have the potential to become a general purpose executor over existing digital devices. To advance them toward real-world use, we envision agents that operate reliably on real devices, execute workflows across platforms, combine GUI interaction with CLI execution, complete long-horizon tasks, proactively initiate useful services, and autonomously improve their capabilities with minimal human effort. Guided by this vision, we present Qwen-UI-Agent , a real-world centric foundation GUI agent spanning mobile, computer-use, web, and DeepSearch environments. Qwen-UI-Agent combines diverse sandbox environments with a large-scale real-device mobile runtime. Its unified action space interleaves GUI operations with CLI execution and generates batched actions in a single model turn. An AutoResearch-style data flywheel uses agents to construct tasks and environments, diagnose failures, and plan subsequent iterations. Online RL support training on trajectories exceeding 100 turns, with over 10,000 concurrent environments accelerating rollout. A lightweight harness layer supports proactive service initiation and stateful workflows across mobile and computer. Across a broad suite of evaluations, Qwen-UI-Agent sets state-of-the-art performance on mobile-use benchmarks while delivering competitive performance on computer- and browser-use tasks against frontier models, including Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.6 Sol. On mobile use, it achieves 82.1% on MobileWorld, 92.2% on MobileWorld-Real, and 97.5% on AndroidDaily. On computer use, it achieves 79.5% on OSWorld-Verified and a 40.0% partial-progress score on OSWorld-v2. On browser use and GUI grounding, it achieves 73.6% on WebArena and 81.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro, respectively. tongyi-mai.github.io/Qwen-UI-Agent Figure 1: Qwen-UI-Agent demonstrates leading or competitive performance across diverse GUI settings. Contents 1 Introduction Graphical user interfaces (GUIs) are the primary interface through which humans access digital services and applications. A capable GUI agent (Zhou et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2025a; Qin et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026) therefore has the potential to become a general purpose executor over existing application ecosystems: it can understand user intent, perceive application states, operate interfaces, and complete tasks without requiring every service to expose a dedicated API. Recent progress in multimodal foundation models has made this direction increasingly practical, leading to rapid improvements in mobile and desktop GUI agents (Cao et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2026). Despite this progress, GUI agents remain largely optimized for simulated benchmarks, leaving a substantial gap between benchmark performance and real-world utility. To bridge this gap, we envision a next generation of GUI agents that operate reliably on real devices, complete long-horizon tasks, carry workflows across platforms, proactively initiate useful services, combine GUI interaction with CLI execution, and continuously evolve their capabilities with less human effort. To realize this vision, we identify six key transitions: (1) From simulated environments to real-device execution. Many GUI agents, especially mobile agents, are…
