articles.title: How to watch the Golden Joystick Awards 2026 tomorrow — including start times and what to expect
articles.content: The Golden Joystick Awards 2026 will air on November 11 at 10AM PT / 1PM ET / 6PM GMT / 7PM CEST Fans can tune in and watch the event live, which will be hosted by Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis actor Alix Wilton Regan The ceremony will announce winners for 25 categories, including Ultimate Game of the Year The winners of the Golden Joystick Awards 2026, one of the biggest ceremonies of the year that celebrates the best games of this year, will be revealed this week - here's when you can tune in. The show is scheduled to begin on November 11 at 10AM PT / 1PM ET / 6PM GMT / 7PM CEST and can be watched live via YouTube , Twitch , TikTok , X , Future Games , and more. Hosted by Dragon Age: Inquisition and Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis actor Alix Wilton Regan, the event will also feature guest presenters from the industry, including Rare composer Chloe Kwok, art and creative director Rex Crowle, Paddle Paddle Paddle developer Mateo Covic, and interviewer, actor, and presenter AlicesPixels. More guest presenters include Resident Evil Requiem actor Nick Apostolides, Star Wars: Galactic Racer actor and Wrestling’s Mr. Charles Crowley, Richard Summers-Calvert, CD Projekt Red production director Malgorzata Mitrega, composer Richard Jacques, and Control Resonant actor, Frankie Kevich. "I’m absolutely thrilled to be your host for this year’s Golden Joystick Awards on November 11th," said Wilton Regan. "We’re celebrating the greatest games of the past 12 months - and, more importantly, the incredibly talented teams who made them happen. The people who put in thousands of hours creating virtual worlds for us to get hopelessly lost in. Get ready for an evening of special guests, spectacular games, and plenty of silly jokes. See you on November 11th when we will unveil your winners!'" Games like 007 First Light , Resident Evil Requiem , Dispatch , Forza Horizon 6 , Big Walk , Crimson Desert , and more are leading this year's nominations across 25 categories , including Ultimate Game of the Year, 22 of which are voted for by the public. "This year’s shortlist offers a fascinating cross-section of our industry in 2026, with the work of small teams of indie developers sitting shoulder to shoulder with titanic gaming franchises like Pokémon and Resident Evil, as well as huge IPs like Star Wars and James Bond," said content director Daniel Dawkins. "The Golden Joystick Awards are the only games awards show chosen by the players - and we can’t wait to see who the public have voted for. Tune in on November 11 to find out the winners and honor the hard work of our industry’s supremely talented developers - in a dazzling ceremony hosted by the wonderful Alix Wilton Regan."
articles.author: Demi Williams

articles.title: The telecoms industry needs to think differently about climate resilience
articles.content: Ten years ago, one of the telecoms industry’s biggest infrastructure challenges was rolling out 4G. Since then, telecoms has transformed – and the environment our infrastructure operates in has changed with it. Summer 2026 was the UK’s hottest on record. In the first nine months of 2026 alone we’ve faced heatwaves, droughts, wildfires, and flash-flood warnings. And climate projections suggest conditions like these will become increasingly familiar. For those of us responsible for the critical national infrastructure people rely on every day, that means thinking about resilience in an entirely different way – shifting the focus from a single network to the continuity of the service people rely on. In telecoms, the physical impacts of climate change can quickly become real issues for our customers . And while operators are already taking steps to prepare their networks – from backup power and cooling to flood protection and longer-term climate risk planning – resilience doesn’t begin and end at the boundaries of an individual network. It has to be thought about in the context of the UK’s digital infrastructure system. The Telecommunications Security Act has already required operators to take a more systemic approach to identifying risks and preparing for disruption. Climate risk now needs the same operational discipline to ensure the connectivity that keeps our economy and national security running stays reliable. We need to think beyond the resilience of individual networks Our networks don’t exist in isolation. We are all connected to a much wider digital ecosystem, and increasingly dependent on other critical infrastructure too. Transport is an obvious example. Telecoms networks depend on roads and transport links remaining accessible so engineers can reach critical sites. That means we need to look beyond the resilience of individual networks and think about the resilience of the system as a whole. Climate risks don’t arrive neatly one at a time, and the impact of an event in one part of our critical national infrastructure can quickly be felt elsewhere. We’ve seen this come to life in extreme weather events. A heatwave can increase cooling demand at the same time as the power system is under strain, and flooding can damage equipment and prevent engineers from reaching it. Each individual operator – whether that be the telecoms company or highways authority – has plans for each disruption scenario. The challenge is that those plans need to work when the same event puts several dependencies under pressure at once. Working together, with government, regulators and the other infrastructure industries we depend on is therefore more vital than ever. Climate adaptation is a strategic national issue. We need to start treating it as one. Adaptation has to change the infrastructure decisions we make today Thinking differently about climate resilience also means thinking differently about the decisions we make today. Identifying climate risks is important, but simply recognizing or reporting them isn’t enough. The real value comes when those risks start to influence how businesses plan, invest and operate. Telecoms infrastructure is built to operate for years, often decades. We can’t predict the exact weather at a particular site in 2040, but we can make decisions now that remain sensible across a credible range of future conditions and identify what would trigger a different course through climate scenario planning. Climate considerations therefore need to be part of long term decisions from capital investment and network planning to executive governance. That isn’t always straightforward. One of the challenges with climate change is its unpredictability. We can see patterns in the science and data , but there isn’t a neat, linear pathway that tells a business exactly what conditions its infrastructure will face in five, ten or twenty years’ time. A lot of the impact we are experiencing today is unchartered territory for humanity as…

articles.title: This free iPhone sleep tracker decodes my 3 a.m. wake ups — and it’s a worthy rival to my Oura Ring 5
articles.content: I've been tracking my sleep with the Oura Ring 5 for the past five months and love its comfortable fit and reliable data, whether I’m monitoring my 3 a.m. wake ups or how long I spend in deep sleep. However, the Oura Ring 5, now from $399 at Amazon , does come at a premium price. Keen to see if it was possible to replicate the accuracy of the Oura without the high cost, I started testing free sleep tracking apps — and discovered one that could hold its own against the best sleep tracker we’ve tested, the Oura Ring 5. The good news? It's completely free, with no hidden costs or trial sign-ups; all you need is a smart phone and a nightstand. Here's how this free iPhone app compares to my $499 Oura Ring 5 (the gold costs more), plus how I'm using its tracking data to better understand my sleep. Looking for a wearable sleep tracker instead? I've rounded up the top sleep trackers you can buy in this year's Black Friday sleep sales , too. The free sleep tracking app that rivals the Oura Ring 5 There are plenty of free sleep tracking apps out there, so I decided to test three popular ones against my Oura Ring 5. The Oura Ring 5 is a luxury smart ring with highly-sophisticated sensor technology that can monitor your sleep cycles , sleep duration , and sleep latency (in other words, how long it takes you to fall asleep). So, not only I was looking a free app that could provide those metrics, I was looking for a free app that could provide those metrics accurately . After the Sleep Cycle and SleepScore apps failed to dazzle me, I didn't hold out much hope for the Sleepwave app, which you can get for free at the App store . Still, a 4.6 star rating out of 5 from over 3,700 user reviews convinced me to give the self-proclaimed "best free sleep tracker app" a go. (Image credit: Future) The Sleepwave app is completely contactless; you simply put your iPhone on your nightstand or mattress. Its sleep tracking relies mostly on movements (for example, from tossing and turning) and breathing, which are picked up by patented motion-sensing technology, as Sleepwave maintains that motion indicates wakefulness. When I woke up after using the app for the first time, my expectations were low. However, comparing the Sleepwave's sleep data to my Oura Ring 5's, I was blown away by the accuracy of its metrics. From my overall sleep duration, my time spent awake during the night (including how long my 3 a.m. wake ups lasted), my sleep stages , and sleep latency. The metrics are all presented in a bright infographic format, which is easy to read. On top of these sleep metrics, the Sleepwave app also includes a smart alarm which wakes you up during light sleep in the morning (when you're naturally more inclined to wake up), so it feels less jarring than being awoken during deep sleep. Plus, thanks to the iPhone's microphone, you can listen to recordings of your bedroom's nocturnal noises, including snoring, vehicles, or pets — handy if you're a light sleeper like me who wants to see whether it's noise that is waking you up at 3 a.m. How Sleepwave's data compares to my Oura Ring 5 (Image credit: Future) As mentioned above, I tested the Sleepwave's accuracy by using the app while wearing my Oura Ring 5 and then comparing the data the next morning. Here's a comparison between data from the Oura Ring and the Sleepwave app, recorded on the same night: Oura Ring 5 vs Sleepwave: Data compared Sleepwave Oura Ring 5 Sleep duration 5 hours 44 minutes 5 hours 41 minutes REM (Dream) 1 hour 17 minutes 1 hour 9 minutes Core (Light) 3 hours 20 minutes 3 hours 21 minutes Deep 1 hour 7 minutes 1 hour 12 minutes Latency 14 minutes 11 minutes I consider a result 5 minutes under or over the Oura Ring metrics as an accurate match. As you can see from the above table, all metrics (apart from the REM sleep metric) fell within the 5-minute threshold — a remarkable result from a free sleep tracker app that's up against a $499 smart ring. articles.title: I used the Pixel 11 Pro XL and Galaxy S26 Ultra for a week. This is the one I’d keep
articles.content: I have this habit of constantly comparing phones, even when I’m perfectly happy with the one I’m using. And when you have some of the best Android phones on the market sitting on your desk, it’s pretty hard to resist switching between them. So, instead of just comparing specs and calling it a day, I spent a week alternating between the Google Pixel 11 Pro XL and the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra to see which one I actually enjoyed using more. And after going back and forth between the two, I think I’ve finally found my favorite.

articles.title: Orbiting ESA satellite plays Doom after receiving voice commands from amateur radio operators on Earth
articles.content: An Oslo radio amateur group, working with Tanagra Space , got a European Space Agency satellite to recognize and launch the 1993 game Doom after catching the word in a voice command sent over the 23 cm band. It took seven attempts, shared with a group in Poland, and the command finally got through on the last two, on the same day in late July. The satellite “understood its assignment,” with the help of a matcher after the 27 MB onboard speech model transcribed the audio, returning a postcard with details of the launch. The satellite, named OPS-SAT PRETTY and flying under the ESA’s OPS-SAT Space Lab program for outside experiments, ran the game in an experiment punningly called PRETTY DOOMed. Doom ran on a different satellite , the OPS-SAT-1, in 2023, but this time is different, as the game was launched with a voice command. (Image credit: Tanagra Space (Doom frame: id Software)) The radio club sending the command in question is LA4O, of the Norwegian Radio Relay League, hams transmitting as part of the experiment. The club’s signal went over 1296 MHz narrowband FM at about 80 W, indicated, using an Icom IC-9700 radio and a Wimo helix antenna at 15.1 dBi, directed by hand. As for the voice, Run 6, the morning pass, used a looped synthesized voice from a keyer, with three of six captures detecting the command. Run 7, the evening pass, used a live operator at a microphone, with one of five usable captures detecting it. The live operator’s command was “LIMA ALFA FOUR OSCAR, PRETTY PLAY DOOM DOOM DOOM, PRETTY PLAY DOOM DOOM DOOM.” The call sign is for legal identification. On board the satellite, the voice is transcribed by a 27 MB quantized English speech-recognition model, picked because it could fit the satellite’s limited computer. The voice was handled by software-defined radio (SDR), which was able to narrow in on the voice and demodulate the source for the speech model. Tuning and demodulating a signal is usually handled by fixed circuits, but using software has the advantage of being mutable with an uploaded update. The voice used this time “was only the test signal,” project lead Georges Labrèche said, and the same setup could handle other things with a new model. The live-voice transcript caught “AND FAR BRIEFLY PLAYING DOOM STEAM DOOM PRECIPATED” with two exact DOOM matches, although one DOOM is enough. Morning detections passed only on fuzzy tolerance with transcripts such as “PLAY DOON.” The achievement is less on the understood side and more about differentiating a voice and a specific command out of the noise in orbit. This can be an iffy business, which is one reason it took seven runs, and being able to update proved useful. The spacecraft heard LA4O, but the output was mostly static, because about 170 kHz reached the FM discriminator for a signal of about ±5 kHz. Offline analysis brought a fix: find the peak within ±100 kHz, shift to baseband, low-pass, and decimate before demodulation. It’s effectively like tuning a car radio to a specific station. Tanagra then reproduced the fix and was able to remove a redundant audio filter. Delivery of the fix took about a week, although the Oslo group’s effort took 59 days and about 7,200 NOK (about $770), pizza included. Tanagra proposes repeat runs that keep the original data and send it back down to Earth, so the researchers can test the live-voice result properly. Better detection may be possible with larger speech models, too, which the team could test on the ground first. Labrèche says the team has demonstrated “a satellite that can listen to any type of radio signal.” Hopefully, the setup can one day detect “mayday” calls and even radio bursts from space.
articles.author: Shane Downing

articles.title: Hunter is killing Google Home and Alexa voice commands and automations in favor of Matter
articles.content: TL;DR Hunter is ending its legacy Google Home and Alexa cloud integrations on January 1, 2027, which will affect voice commands and automations. Matter will keep eligible HunterSMART fans connected, but some models will need firmware updates or replacement hardware. Physical controls and supported HunterSMART app features will continue working, although hardware upgrade costs and rollout timelines remain unclear. Matter is supposed to make smart homes less complicated, breaking down the walls between competing ecosystems and letting devices from different brands speak the same language. But for Hunter ceiling fan owners, getting everyone on the same page comes with an unexpected twist: the company is retiring the very connections that currently let its fans work with Google Home and Amazon Alexa . And there’s now a deadline attached. Hunter has been laying the groundwork for this change for months. The company started sending out emails in July (via Reddit ) revealing plans to bring Matter support to eligible smart ceiling fans, potentially through firmware updates or replacement Wi-Fi hardware. What sounded like a straightforward connectivity upgrade at the time now has another side to the story: existing Google Home and Alexa integrations are on borrowed time.

articles.title: Apple Watch Black Friday deals: I've run hundreds of miles with the Apple Watch Ultra 4, and it has $100 off right now
articles.content: We’ve still got three weeks to go until Black Friday, but as always, the deals have started early. I’ve been writing about the Apple Watch for the past decade, so I’ll be keeping an eye on the best deals to grab as we get closer to Black Friday. Today, the best Black Friday deal is on the Apple Watch Ultra 4, which has $100 off, discounted to $699 on Amazon . The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is Apple’s newest watch, so it’s surprising to see such a huge discount this early. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is Apple’s newest smartwatch, launching in September. It has Apple’s newest heart rate monitor and Readiness score, as well as the longest battery life of any Apple Watch. View Deal The Apple Watch Ultra 4 looks pretty much identical to last year’s Apple Watch Ultra 3, but it’s a far better choice for most people. It has a new heart rate monitor, a readiness score to help you know when to push and when to rest, two days of battery life for the first time, and new Audio Intelligence features. During testing, I’ve been impressed with the heart rate monitor on the Apple Watch Ultra 4. When looking at the two monitors side-by-side, the Ultra 4 and the Apple Watch Series 12 have a “32-petal design,” whereas older watches had a two-petal design. This refers to the spoke-like lines coming out of the electrode (Image credit: Future) Heart rate data lies at the heart of a lot of health features on the Apple Watch, including HRV, workouts, and ovulation prediction. With the Apple Watch Ultra 4, the new heart rate monitor, along with the S-11 chip, measures your heart rate every five seconds, all day long. You’ll also be able to see your Recovery HRV score, which shows signs of stress and recovery, as well as your overall HRV, which offers insights into your overall health. With a 50-hour battery life, extended to 84 hours in low power mode, this also has the best battery life of any Apple Watch. I was able to wear it for a full marathon without worrying about running out of charge. With $100 off, this is a great price for the latest model. I doubt it’ll get much cheaper as we get nearer to Black Friday.

articles.title: Royal Navy stands up first autonomous boat squadron
articles.content: Britain’s Royal Navy has formally commissioned its first uncrewed boat squadron, operating seaborne drones on front-line operations as part of its “Hybrid Navy” strategy. The force says the 1 st Autonomous Squadron officially entered active service on November 5 at a ceremony in Portsmouth Naval Base. It comprises around 180 personnel, about the same as a Type 23 frigate, split into two watches to enable operations around the clock. This active squadron replaces Project Beehive, the navy’s experimental program to build a fleet of autonomous and remotely operated vessels, through which it obtained 20 uncrewed boats from UK-based Kraken Technology Group. The force is understood to be using both Kraken’s K3 Scout, and the SM400 from SYOS Aerospace, known by the Royal Navy as the Rattler. The K3 Scout is an 8.4 m boat capable of 55 knots and can carry a payload of up to 600 kg. It has a range of up to 650 nautical miles and endurance of up to 7 days. The maker describes it as capable of a range of missions, including anti-ship and anti-submarine to detecting and countering other drones and even casualty evacuation. The Rattler boat is 7.2 m and has a 500 kg modular bay, with a range of up to 950 nautical miles. It was used last year in a demonstration during which 5 of the uncrewed boats were remotely-piloted to escort patrol ship HMS Tyne and mine countermeasures mothership HMS Stirling Castle Part of the new squadron’s mission will be to act as pathfinder for drone operations, working on bringing additional types of uncrewed surface vessel (USVs) into fleet service and conducting a range of operations alongside other organizations – both as single vessels and as part of a task group. The “Hybrid Navy” concept was outlined by First Sea Lord General Sir Gwyn Jenkins earlier this year, who made the case that uncrewed vessels would be vital in filling the gaps left by the Royal Navy’s much depleted surface fleet. Speaking at the launch of the autonomous squadron, Fleet Commander Vice-Admiral Steve Moorhouse hailed it as an historic occasion, but warned that the seas are becoming more contested, more dangerous and harder to operate in. “A hybrid navy is about giving our people better tools. It means more reach, more striking power and more options,” he stated. Last week, the force also launched strike drones from one of its aircraft carriers for the first time. Nyan one-way drones made by BAE Systems were launched from the deck, as well as a Tekever AR5 fixed-wing uncrewed aircraft, the same kind the British Army has selected to replace its troublesome Watchkeeper fleet. Elsewhere, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) says it has launched a British-built satellite called Titania into orbit, claiming it “gives the Armed Forces a new pair of eyes in space.” However, the original purpose of the orbiter was understood to be to test high-speed optical communications from low Earth orbit directly to Earth, using laser beams that are harder to intercept than radio links. Titania is the second satellite in the UK’s growing constellation of military satellites in orbit, following the launch of Tyche in October, and will be operated by UK Space Command as part of the ISTARI* program. The latter aims to deliver satellites and supporting ground systems to expand space-based intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, the MoD said. However, while the satellite is British-made, it got into space via an American rocket, riding on SpaceX’s Transporter-18 mission. ® * What is it with the tech industry and Tolkien references?
articles.author: Dan Robinson

articles.title: I Followed the Textbook Fix for PageSpeed and My Site Got Slower
articles.content: I wanted a perfect mobile PageSpeed score for my side project, a free game backlog tracker. It started at 86. Within an hour, it was 77. By the end of the afternoon, it was 99. Here is the part of that story that taught me something. The advice everyone gives My report listed “render-blocking requests” with an estimated saving of 840 ms. The biggest blocker was the Google Fonts stylesheet. Every performance article gives the same answer: load it asynchronously. <link rel="stylesheet" href="..." media="print" onload="this.media='all'"> I applied it, rebuilt, ran the test again. The score fell from 86 to 77. First Contentful Paint did not improve. Cumulative Layout Shift went from 0.001 to 0.131. The fonts now arrived after the first paint, text rendered in a fallback font, then jumped when the real font loaded. I had not removed the cost; I had moved it from “wait” to “shift”, and the metric that punishes shifting is worth more points than I expected. I stopped guessing and read the report properly Instead of trying a third trick, I read what the tool listed under diagnostics, line by line, and checked each with curl . 1. Nothing was compressed. The report said text compression was missing. I did not believe it, because my reverse proxy config has encode gzip zstd . So I tested: curl -sI -H "Accept-Encoding: gzip" https://example.com/ No Content-Encoding header. Not on the HTML, not on the 76 KB stylesheet. In production, the proxy was not actually in front of the Node server. One line of Express middleware fixed it: app.use(require('compression')()) 2. A hidden @import . A second font request appeared in the waterfall that I had never added to the page. It came from a scoped style block inside a “Buy me a coffee” button component, where someone (me, months ago) had written @import url(' https://fonts.googleapis.com/...') . The bundler had merged that into the main stylesheet, so my entire CSS was waiting on a third-party server. I replaced that font with a system stack. 3. The headline was waiting for its animation. My hero used a fade-in with opacity: 0 at the start, 0.8 seconds long, with a stagger delay of up to 0.85 s. The browser cannot count an invisible element as the largest paint, so the largest contentful paint was literally behind an animation. I shortened it to 0.35 s with no stagger and a nearly-visible starting state. Self-hosting the fonts, the safe way With the real problems fixed, I went back to fonts and did it properly: Downloaded the woff2 files and inlined the @font-face rules in the HTML. Preloaded only the Latin subsets of the two families used above the fold. Left other scripts (Cyrillic, Greek, Vietnamese) as separate files with unicode-range , because the site has 12 languages and those only load when needed. The numbers Before After Performance 86 99 First Contentful Paint 3.0 s 1.4 s Largest Contentful Paint 3.2 s 2.0 s Layout shift 0.001 0.023 Accessibility also went from 95 to 100, after I raised the contrast of the footer text. What I would tell my past self Verify the basics with curl before trusting a config file. The most valuable fix was the one that needed no cleverness: compression was simply off. Search your build output for @import . Third-party requests hide in places you stopped looking. Be suspicious of generic advice. “Load fonts async” is correct for some sites and harmful for others. Measure after every single change, one at a time. Do not animate your biggest element in from invisible. It looks nice and costs you LCP. The score is a proxy. What I actually care about is that the page now appears in about a second and a half on a mid-range phone on a slow connection, and that I can explain why.

articles.title: This Googlebook is driving me crazy
articles.content: Right now, Googlebooks make more sense for Google than they do for users. After trying for years to bring Android features to Chromebooks, Google decided to start over with Android as the foundation for a new laptop operating system. The first wave of Googlebooks are high-end laptops (priced $900 and up), with Google pitching them as the ultimate computers for Android enthusiasts. But in their current form, Googlebooks are a disjointed mess, with websites and apps that don’t work quite right and AI features that aren’t fully fleshed out. While having a single operating system and app platform across laptops and mobile devices might make life easier for Google, it doesn’t yet translate to a better experience than the Chromebooks that Google aims to replace. Android’s not ready for laptops For the past month I’ve been using Acer’s Googlebook 14 , which is the cheapest Googlebook at $900, and the only one whose touchscreen flips around into tablet mode. I have no major complaints about the hardware, which has a featherweight 2.51-pound chassis, a rich 120 Hz 3K OLED screen, and a smooth trackpad (albeit a “diving board” type whose click mechanism stiffens at the top edge). My frustrations are more on the software side, where Android isn’t ready to carry a real laptop workload. While Google is pushing developers to optimize their Android apps for large screens, keyboards, and trackpads, Google itself hasn’t always bothered to do so. The preloaded version of Gmail, for instance, is not an optimized Android app, but rather a web-based desktop app powered by the Chrome browser. Same goes for Google Docs, Drive, Meet, and YouTube. Tapping the menu button in these apps reveals a “Running in Chrome” disclaimer, and any Chrome extensions you install will apply to these apps as well. This wouldn’t be a major concern if the web apps worked the way they’re supposed to. In Gmail, though, cursor hover controls don’t work, so you can’t quickly trash or archive messages line by line in the inbox. In Google Drive, documents open in a Chrome browser tab, while the same documents open in their own windows via Google Docs or Sheets. And if you try to select text in Google Docs using the touchscreen, the comment button pops up directly over the right text selector, making it unreachable. Third-party Android apps can also have issues. Signing into Slack bounces me out to a Chrome tab, which then fails to authenticate back inside the Android app, so the only way to gain access is by manually entering a URL and password for each workplace. Even then, Slack’s Android app is poorly optimized, without the desktop version’s persistent sidebar. Video apps still feel unfinished on Googlebooks as well. Those that Google deems “optimized for desktop,” such as Netflix and Disney+, will automatically open in full screen, which is jarring but at least fits the use case of watching video. Others, such as Fox One and NFL, open in a floating desktop window, and clicking their full screen icons accomplishes nothing. You’re actually supposed to ignore that button, highlight the maximize button in the window controls, then click the little “Full Screen” icon. Optimized or not, none of these apps support always-visible picture-in-picture mode like their mobile counterparts. One last nitpick, admittedly a niche one: Bookmarklets don’t work on Googlebooks. I keep more than dozen of these in my browser’s address bar, which allows me to launch site-specific searches, create page excerpts, find archived versions of web pages, and remove “sticky” page elements. Not being able to use them on the Googlebook is a reminder that you’re not quite getting a full Chrome desktop experience. The app situation will likely improve over time. When I started using the Googlebook, it wouldn’t let me install the Bluesky app…

articles.title: Before You Spend More on Ads, Find Out What Happened to Your Last 300 Leads
articles.content: I worked with a company selling and installing photovoltaic systems for homeowners just as a government subsidy program was preparing to bring a sharp increase in demand. At the time, the business was receiving between 10 and 20 leads a month. The website needed substantial improvements, enquiries came through different channels, and the sales team had no CRM to manage them in one place. Preparing for the campaigns involved working on the commercial process alongside the marketing activities. The company needed a way to collect enquiries, make them available to sales and keep track of what happened after the first contact. These decisions had to be made while the website, campaigns and sales procedures were being developed. During the campaign, the company generated approximately 10,000 leads, around 3,300 per month. The government program created exceptional demand, while the advertising campaigns and website improvements helped capture that interest. My role covered marketing strategy and the coordination of its implementation. I managed the Meta campaigns, coordinated the agency responsible for Google Ads and worked with the web developers on the website. On the commercial side, I worked with the founder and sales team on selecting and integrating the CRM, defining how enquiries would be handled and preparing the information salespeople needed in their conversations. The volume eventually reached a level that would have been difficult to manage through the previous arrangements. The preparation of the commercial process became an important part of making that increase manageable. A Request Can Pass Through Several Systems Before Anyone Calls When someone fills in a contact form, the information may pass through several systems before reaching a salesperson. The website receives the submission, an advertising platform may register a conversion, an automation tool transfers the data, and the CRM creates or updates a record. Each system records a different stage. A successful conversion in the advertising account tells marketing that somebody completed the intended action. The sales team needs the information to appear in the right place, with enough context to understand the enquiry and continue the conversation. The difference becomes important when the number of requests increases. At 10 or 20 enquiries a month, a small team may be able to manage follow-up through emails, spreadsheets and direct conversations. People can compensate for an imperfect process because the volume is relatively low. When several hundred requests arrive in a week, keeping track of them requires a shared system and clear responsibilities. There is also a reporting limitation worth understanding. A CRM can show the records it has received, including their status and assigned owner. An enquiry that disappears before reaching the CRM may be absent from its reports altogether. For that reason, it is useful to keep a record of submissions at the point where they enter the process, such as the website form or the advertising platform, and compare it with the records created in the CRM. The comparison helps identify requests that were submitted successfully but did not reach the intended destination. The company also needs a consistent way to distinguish legitimate enquiries from internal tests, spam and duplicates. Otherwise, the numbers can become difficult to reconcile, especially when the same person contacts the business through more than one channel. These details affect the quality of information available to both marketing and sales. They become increasingly relevant when management is making decisions based on lead volumes and campaign performance. What We Connected, and What Had to Be Decided Alongside It In the renewable energy project, we brought enquiries from several sources into a common CRM. Website forms, paid campaigns and other communication channels needed to feed into a commercial process that the sales team could use consistently.…

articles.title: AI is changing cancer treatment — and a new breakthrough shows just how far we've come
articles.content: AI is already integrated into our lives in many ways. It's changing the way we work, search and communicate. And while that kind of AI use may not be for everyone, perhaps one thing we can all agree on is how it is progressing medicine through breakthroughs that may have not happened without it. At least, not as quickly. Researchers are using AI to understand cancer at a level of detail that would have been difficult to imagine just a decade ago. Rather than treating every patient with the same type of cancer in the same way, scientists are working toward treatments based on the unique genetic makeup of each person's tumor. And there are encouraging signs that more personalized cancer treatments could make a real difference. In October, researchers reported promising Phase 3 clinical trial results for an experimental personalized cancer vaccine developed by Moderna and Merck. When combined with the immunotherapy drug Keytruda, the vaccine reduced the relative risk of melanoma recurrence or death by 42% compared with Keytruda alone. The vaccine isn't FDA-approved yet, and the trial doesn't establish that generative AI invented the treatment. But the results offer an important example of what personalized cancer medicine can achieve. Meanwhile, AI is helping researchers tackle another part of the challenge: understanding exactly what makes one person's cancer different from another's. AI could help doctors find the right treatment for each patient (Image credit: National Cancer Institute) One of the biggest challenges in treating cancer is that two people with the same diagnosis can respond very differently to the same medication. That's partly because cancer isn't a single disease. Even tumors that appear similar can have different genetic mutations, making one treatment effective for one patient and less useful for another. A study within the last six months highlights that instead of relying solely on patterns found across thousands of patients, researchers can increasingly investigate the biological characteristics of a specific person's tumor. AI is particularly useful because it can analyze enormous quantities of genetic information and identify relationships that might otherwise be missed. The National Cancer Institute has already demonstrated one approach. Its PERCEPTION AI tool analyzes gene activity in individual cancer cells to predict whether certain drugs might work. This is a significant breakthrough since tumors can contain different populations of cells. A drug might successfully attack some while leaving others behind, potentially allowing the cancer to return or develop resistance. Tools like PERCEPTION could eventually help doctors understand those differences before deciding which treatment to recommend. Google DeepMind is helping speed up drug discovery (Image credit: Google) Another significant development involves AlphaFold , the AI system developed by Google DeepMind. Proteins play a central role in how cells function, including how cancer develops and spreads. Understanding their three-dimensional structures can help scientists determine how potential drugs might interact with them. Traditionally, identifying those structures could take years of laboratory work. AlphaFold can predict many protein structures in minutes, giving researchers a much faster starting point. Google DeepMind has made predictions for more than 200 million protein structures available to researchers worldwide. And while that doesn't mean AlphaFold can automatically create a safe or effective cancer drug, scientists still need to determine whether predicted interactions work in laboratory experiments and, eventually, in patients. It can however, possibly help narrow narrow down the possibilities, potentially saving researchers significant time during the earliest stages of drug development. articles.title: Building Verifiable Shared‑State Infrastructure for Decentralized AI Agents
articles.content: Imagine a network of autonomous AI agents operating across different processes and infrastructure. One agent updates shared data, another makes a decision based on that data, and a third executes the next step in a workflow. What happens if a process crashes, a message is retried, or two operations conflict? These are not problems that better models alone can solve. They are distributed-systems challenges involving persistence, coordination, recovery, and state integrity. As AI applications become more distributed, these infrastructure concerns become increasingly relevant. Agents need dependable ways to access shared information, recover from failures, and determine whether recorded state changes can be verified. HyperStack is an attempt to make the underlying infrastructure reusable. Rather than building a database exclusively for AI, it is developing a distributed database and compute stack on AO and HyperBEAM. Decentralized AI is one potential application of this infrastructure, alongside other real-time distributed workloads. The Problem: Coordination Requires More Than Intelligence AI systems are increasingly being designed around multiple agents, tools, and independent processes. These components may share data, operate asynchronously, and depend on the results of previous operations. This creates familiar distributed-systems problems. An agent may read outdated information. Concurrent operations may produce conflicting updates. A process may fail before a write is durably recorded. A retry may accidentally execute an operation more than once. After a failure, the system needs a reliable way to determine which changes were accepted and which were actually persisted. These issues are not unique to AI. Distributed databases and real-time applications have dealt with similar challenges for decades. However, as developers build more complex agent workflows, they must still decide how to handle shared state, retries, persistence, and recovery across their own infrastructure. A conventional centralized database may be sufficient for many applications. The challenge becomes more interesting when an application needs to distribute its infrastructure across multiple nodes or independently operated environments, while making its state and durability guarantees explicit. This is where HyperStack sees an opportunity. What Others May Overlook: The Infrastructure Beneath AI Much of the discussion around AI focuses on model capabilities, inference performance, and compute availability. These are important, but they are only part of the system. An application can use a powerful model and still fail because its agents operate on inconsistent information or because a critical update cannot be recovered after a crash. The same principle applies outside AI. Multiplayer applications, real-time services, and distributed workloads all depend on reliable mechanisms for managing state across processes. Our perspective is that these mechanisms should be reusable infrastructure rather than something every application must independently reconstruct. HyperStack explores this idea by combining distributed persistence, recovery mechanisms, and state verification within a general-purpose stack built on AO and HyperBEAM. The goal is not to claim that every AI application needs a decentralized database. It is to investigate whether reusable distributed infrastructure can help developers build applications that require more explicit durability and verifiability guarantees. How HyperStack Approaches the Problem HyperStack combines AO and HyperBEAM with a distributed database and compute architecture built using lua/WASM, and Erlang/BEAM. At a high level, the stack separates request sequencing, data persistence, and state verification into distinct responsibilities. articles.title: Anthropic unveils Claude Fable 5.2, Mythos 5.2 with coding gains and lower prices
articles.content: Anthropic has introduced Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, claiming significant improvements in handling complex software engineering tasks while cutting API prices by 20% compared with the previous versions. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 share the same underlying model but have different safeguards. Fable is broadly available, while direct access to Mythos is restricted to vetted cybersecurity and life sciences organizations to limit potential misuse. The models are both priced at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, down from $10 and $50, respectively. Anthropic said the newer versions can generate output up to 30% faster than their predecessors. The company reported substantial gains in coding performance. Fable 5.2 scored 49.1% on the FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark at its Xhigh effort setting, compared with 32.4% for Fable 5.1. The benchmark assesses whether maintainers of open-source projects would accept AI-generated changes to their code. Performance and costs could entice enterprises The models’ improved performance and lower prices could make long-running AI agents viable for software migrations and scientific research, according to Lian Jye Su , chief analyst at Omdia. Higher task completion rates could further reduce deployment costs, he said. Anthropic said Fable 5.2 at its “High effort” setting achieved a coding benchmark score comparable to Opus 5.5 at its highest setting, at roughly half the cost per task. The comparison suggests that Fable could be more economical for some demanding assignments, although the savings would depend on the workload and effort setting. “Anthropic has cut the price of a token, not the price of a thought,” said Sanchit Vir Gogia , chief analyst at Greyhound Research. He urged CIOs to treat AI processing effort as a budget consideration and measure costs against successfully completed tasks. Anthropic also recommends Opus 5.5 for most coding and knowledge work, with Fable and Mythos intended for more demanding assignments. Reliability challenges persist In an internal experiment, an Anthropic engineer tasked Fable 5.2 with building a prototype operating system. The model coordinated more than 1,000 subagents over eight days and produced software that could boot on a laptop. Su said the improvements bring enterprises closer to highly autonomous software development, although widespread deployment will depend on addressing persistent operational limitations. “Reliability remains an issue without human supervision,” Su said. Coordinating multiple AI agents across enterprise tools and internal teams also remains difficult, he added. Organizations will need to monitor agent activity and run these systems in appropriately isolated environments. Critical changes should remain subject to human approval , with sufficient visibility into agent behavior to support audits. Pareekh Jain , CEO of Pareekh Consulting, said complex legacy systems and the need to meet business requirements could limit how much software development enterprises can delegate to AI agents. Faster vulnerability discovery raises concerns Anthropic said Mythos 5.2 identified 89.6% of vulnerabilities in its internal CVE Rediscovery evaluation, compared with 78.3% for Mythos 5.1. Conducted against 1,829 previously disclosed vulnerabilities, the test assessed whether models could independently rediscover flaws in software snapshots taken before the vulnerabilities were fixed. The company said Mythos 5.2 was also better at reproducing vulnerabilities and developing fixes. Anthropic has restricted direct access to Mythos 5.2 through its verification programs. However, Claude Enterprise customers can use the model’s vulnerability detection capabilities through Claude Security without joining those programs, the company said. According to Su, “Mythos 5.2 shifts the balance towards defenders in controlled enterprise settings.” Jain, however, cautioned that advances in AI-powered vulnerability discovery could also help…

articles.title: Microsoft teaches schools that free email was just a phase
articles.content: Microsoft is retiring its free education email service, leaving schools, colleges, and universities facing new licensing bills if they want to keep students' mailboxes. The company announced plans last week to retire Office 365 A1, the Student Use Benefit program, and free Exchange Online for Alumni. The changes generally take effect at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028. Office 365 A1 provides eligible institutions with web-based Office applications, Teams, and email at no charge. Its replacement, Microsoft 365 Education A0, excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also depends on paid faculty licensing and students actively using Windows devices for education. A spokesperson for the UK's Department for Education told The Register : "We are disappointed that Microsoft has made this decision. However, we are pleased to have successfully negotiated some additional concessions for the UK, giving schools, colleges and universities the time they need to be able to successfully transition to new licensing agreements." An industry insider said the loss of free Microsoft-hosted email could add thousands to institutions' bills. Another organization noted "significant concerns… around affordability, equitable treatment across the sector, and the longer-term implications of the changes." A spokesperson for UK education technology body Jisc told The Register that its "focus has been on ensuring that UK education providers are well supported and have sufficient time to assess their options." "We continue working closely with Microsoft and sector partners to support those discussions and help institutions make informed decisions about their future requirements." Also being retired are free Exchange Online for Alumni - which lets graduates retain their mailboxes - and the Student Use Benefit, providing student licenses at no additional charge when institutions purchase qualifying faculty licenses. Microsoft plans a paid alumni replacement. The Windows giant is also changing storage entitlements and introducing Microsoft 365 Education A7, its "most advanced education offering," which adds AI, security, governance, and device-management features. Asked why it was removing those services from the free tier, Microsoft framed the overhaul as a response to institutions' changing needs. A spokesperson told The Register : "Education institutions are evaluating AI, security, privacy, governance, and teaching and learning as connected priorities rather than separate technology decisions. "Microsoft is updating the portfolio now to provide a clearer path from foundational access to advanced capabilities, while enabling institutions to adopt technology according to their needs and readiness. This evolution reflects both the value Microsoft 365 Education has gained since the last pricing change nearly a decade ago and the structure of the new portfolio. "Microsoft's broader goal is not technology adoption for its own sake. It is to support AI and digital experiences that strengthen learning, preserve educator judgment and give institutions the controls they need to manage data, privacy, and responsible use." Office 365 A1 stopped accepting new web-direct orders on November 5, 2026, with partner-channel sales ending on May 1, 2027. Retirement is scheduled for January 1, 2028, but existing agreements remain valid through their current terms. Institutions that need continued service must move to replacement licenses at the applicable renewal or contract expiry. ®

articles.title: GENZA Brings Vibe-First Dating to the United States, Starting in Los Angeles
articles.content: Los Angeles, United States, November 9th, 2026/TechnologyWire/-- GENZA , a gamified dating app built for Gen Z adults, today announced its U.S. launch, with Los Angeles leading its first wave. GENZA is built on a simple premise: the people who matter most in our lives were never chosen from a photo. What makes them special is how they make people feel — the humor, the chemistry, that sense of being understood. Tapping into Gen Z’s shift toward “chalance” dating, an approach that values openness and genuine effort over playing it cool, GENZA reverses the traditional dating-app model. Instead of endless swiping and split-second judgments based on appearance, users connect through interactive experiences that reveal personality, shared values and emotional compatibility. Profile photos unlock once your bond level reaches 100%. “Dating has become so focused on the perfect first impression that people spend more time choosing photos and writing bios than actually getting to know each other. But chemistry is about more than how someone looks on a screen. It’s how they think, react, laugh and connect when you do something together. For many young people, swiping through photos is the only kind of online dating they’ve ever known. We want to offer something different. Gen Z already uses games to connect, collaborate and build friendships, so why shouldn’t dating work the same way? With GENZA, we want people to feel comfortable being themselves, discover whether there’s real chemistry and let the photos come later. It’s not about hiding who you are — it’s about giving someone the chance to discover you before they make up their mind,” said Val Klimov, Founder and Chief Strategy Officer of GENZA. The app has no traditional bios or profile questionnaires. Users express themselves through customizable 3D avatars that serve as their visual identities within GENZA’s interactive environment. At the core of the app is the Vibe Code, a personal compatibility profile that each user builds through interactive self-discovery quests. The quests capture a person’s values, preferences and behavioral patterns. GENZA’s AI then analyzes the profile across 30 grounded personality traits drawn from established personality research to suggest two potential matches at a time, based on emotional compatibility, shared values and energy. Once matched, users can chat and play co-op games designed for two in a private 3D room. In “Last $50,” for example, the pair gets a virtual $50 budget to spend on a random lineup of in-game items, from a pet rock and a ring light to 100 rubber ducks. After revealing their choices, they get a short, playful take from GENZA’s AI. There’s no winning or losing. The fun is in discovering what someone chooses, who they choose it for, and what those choices reveal about their personality. Photos remain blurred at first and unlock as the connection develops. The goal is not to replace in-person dating with a virtual experience. GENZA uses play as a starting point for discovering mutual interest, helping people build connections they can take into real life when the time feels right. Verification features are also designed to help keep profiles authentic and reduce fake accounts. The idea reflects a broader shift in how younger generations approach social connections. According to the Entertainment Software Association’s (ESA) 2026 Essential Facts report, 88% of Gen Z players believe video games are a great way to bring people together, while 87% say they help build relationships. The organization’s 2025 report also found that 63% of Gen Z players had met a good friend or significant other through video games. GENZA brings this power of shared experiences into dating, helping people discover chemistry through interaction, collaboration and play. “As a Gen Zer, I didn’t want to build yet another app where the most interesting thing about you has to fit into a few photos and a short bio. With GENZA, we started with a different…

articles.title: Rian Johnson’s new camera app shows what’s missing from iPhone photos
articles.content: Last week saw an unexpected hit on the iPhone App Store: a $12.99 camera app without a free trial or a subscription. Chromagraph Camera shot to the top of the paid Photo & Video charts after Knives Out and Star Wars: The Last Jedi director Rian Johnson revealed that he had assigned his longtime cinematographer, Steve Yedlin, to work on his dream photo app for the iPhone. Johnson, who partnered with Yedlin on every feature film throughout his career—from 2005’s Brick to last year’s latest Knives Out mystery, Wake Up Dead Man —suggested that this was a project he’d wanted to exist for a while. “So I recently badgered my cinematographer @steveyedlin into making my ideal iPhone still camera app,” Johnson wrote on X. “It shoots RAW, bypasses the iPhone’s look processing and instead uses the same image processing we use on our movies.” Growing discontent The pitch speaks to a growing discontent with the way the default camera app on the iPhone handles image processing. Apple’s computational photography pipeline is incredibly good at making sure you don’t miss the moment, and at rescuing challenging exposures, blending several frames together at once so you don’t blow out highlights or lose details in the shadows. But flattening the actual world like that comes at the expense of traditional photographic character, leaving images feeling artificially sharpened and reliant on HDR. Yedlin is uniquely qualified to rethink how a smartphone camera might turn light into a final photo. In filmmaking circles, he is well-known for his research into color science. His Display Prep Demo in 2015 was influential in showing how a particular filmic look isn’t unique to actual celluloid or a certain camera brand, but something that can be replicated by transforming raw digital sensor data. Yedlin argued that creators should be the authors of their own looks, sculpting elements of the image like grain, tonal rolloff and halation, or the glow that surrounds bright light sources on film. Chromagraph showcases that philosophy on a smaller scale. Combined with work from color science programmer Eric Cameron, it takes the iPhone’s raw sensor data and tweaks it to Yedlin’s specific taste. You don’t see the effect while framing your shot in the viewfinder; the effect is applied after you capture the image. But because Chromagraph stores the original raw files, you can later tweak parameters like tone, grain, and halation after the fact without losing image quality, then export the JPEG to your camera roll. That’s a world away from traditional photo filters. Even Apple’s ProRAW format still retains elements of the iPhone’s multiframe merging. The look won’t be for everyone. Next to a full-resolution ProRAW shot, you’re inevitably going to get a softer, grainier image that will often blow out the highlights. The app’s user interface could also use some work, as it doesn’t feel fully native to iOS. But in my testing, I’ve been struck by how cohesive Chromagraph feels across a variety of situations. It’s like the app turns the iPhone into a singular 35mm point-and-shoot camera with a well-chosen film stock. I’ve rarely been disappointed with the results. “The custom look is opinionated,” Yedlin told Newsshooter . “It’s just the nuanced and idiosyncratic rendering of tonality and chromaticity (as well as grain and halation) that Rian, Eric, and I personally like. And the grading knobs allow you to make pretty dramatic adjustments while keeping within that overall core look.” Not the first try Chromagraph isn’t the first attempt to bring a more traditionally photographic style to smartphone imagery. For years now, Chinese phone makers Oppo and Xiaomi—in partnership with pro camera titans Hasselblad and Leica, respectively—have deployed tasteful image processing pipelines right in their default camera apps. The standard Leica Authentic mode on Xiaomi phones is particularly good; this year’s Xiaomi 17 Ultra even included an option to directly emulate…
articles.author: Sam Byford

articles.title: Google’s 2027 foldable app push has readers hopeful, but not convinced
articles.content: Foldable phones offer consumers novel hardware that is not only great party pieces but also provide sensible solutions for the practical problems of digital life. Want a large display that folds into the size of a traditional smartphone? Get a foldable . There is perhaps one issue with Android foldables: app optimization. There are plenty of Android apps that don’t support large-screen formats . These are guilty of stretching elements out of proportion or simply not making use of all that screen real estate.

articles.title: Google is closing the door on third-party Fitbit apps and clock faces this month
articles.content: TL;DR Google is removing third-party apps and clock faces from the Fitbit App Gallery starting November 28, 2026. The change affects older Fitbit Sense, Versa, and Ionic smartwatches, leaving only Google and Fitbit offerings available. Existing third-party installations will keep working, but deleting them or factory resetting your watch will permanently remove access. Owning an older Fitbit smartwatch increasingly feels like watching its once-crowded toolbox empty out, one feature at a time. Google has already trimmed music features , restricted third-party apps on newer models, and removed familiar Fitbit perks during the move to Google Health . Now, another door is closing, and this time even a factory reset could cost you something you can’t get back. Starting November 28, 2026, Google’s Fitbit App Gallery will stop offering third-party apps and clock faces, leaving only those made by Fitbit and Google. The company confirmed the change in an official community announcement , with an updated support page spelling out what it means for existing installations and future downloads.
articles.author: Hillary Keverenge
articles.fingerprint: apps clock closing door faces fitbit google month party third

articles.title: Boston Dynamics Adds Wheels to Atlas Humanoid
articles.content: Boston Dynamics has equipped its Atlas humanoid with wheels, allowing the robot to rapidly roll across flat terrain while still using its articulated legs to navigate obstacles and uneven surfaces. "The 'experiment' combined classical model-based motor control with whole-body reinforcement learning to maintain dynamic stability across unstructured, real-world terrain," reports The Robot Report. From the report: In addition to learning how to move with wheels for feet, Atlas also performs pirouettes and various aggressive actuation maneuvers. This demonstrates that Atlas can smoothly switch between fast rolling on flat terrain and articulated legged motion over obstacles or irregular surfaces. [Andy Wu, controls engineer for Atlas at Boston Dynamics] trained the system in sim. The system learned all of the behaviors in sim and executed them in real life, with surprising accuracy, according to Wu. Wu said converting Atlas' locomotion style was "wonderfully simple." A single custom adapter mounts an off-the-shelf scooter rim onto Atlas' existing ankle actuator, and that's the only new part in the whole build. Because Atlas was designed from the start to be produced at high volume and to be easy to service, Wu said the retrofit was about as involved as swapping a wheel on a bicycle. The software side was just as straightforward, he said. Each wheel is modeled as an "ankle" that can spin continuously, so all Wu had to do was take the baseline robot model and swap the feet out for wheels. The next question that Wu intends to answer is the policy response to failed actuators. This is key to safety and to understanding how the system will respond to a system failure. The primary takeaway for Wu and the controls engineering team at Boston Dynamics is to understand control synergy. The video demonstrates that merging classical motor controls (for baseline stability) with whole-body RL (for reactive adaptation) yields superior real-world agility compared to using either method alone. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Meta Releases Muse Ember, a 1M-Context Model for High-Volume Agent Work
articles.content: Meta Superintelligence Labs has released Muse Ember , its smallest and most efficient model. Meta Muse Ember is a hosted multimodal reasoning model built for the repetitive steps inside agents. Meta lists tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction and long document parsing as targets. It scores 36 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, level with Claude Haiku 5.5 at max effort. Meta puts its cost at about $0.14 per index task. TL;DR Size: 1M-token context window, up to 512K output tokens. Runs on: Meta’s hosted infrastructure only (Meta Model API and Muse Code). Weights are private, so there is no local GPU, laptop or quantized option. Performance: Ties Claude Haiku 5.5 (max) at 36 on the AA Intelligence Index, ahead of GPT-6 Luna (28). Best: AutomationBench-AA at 37.8, versus 20.2 for GPT-6 Luna and 13.9 for Claude Haiku 5.5. Worst: FrontierCode 2.0-AA at 27.2, behind Claude Haiku 5.5 at 34.9. Bottom line: Best: Haiku-level intelligence at $0.136 per task versus $0.411. Worst: closed weights and weaker on mergeable real-repo code. What is Meta Muse Ember? Muse Ember is a small reasoning model from Meta for high-volume agent subtasks. It is the fourth model under the Muse brand , after Spark, Glimmer and Wonder. Meta positions it below its larger models. Muse Wonder handles the hardest problems and Muse Spark covers coding and agentic workflows. Ember takes repeatable coding and agent tasks at scale. Meta’s own framing: Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume. How does Muse Ember work? Muse Ember is the first model Meta trained using Muse Wonder Full, its largest model. The model natively accepts text, images, audio and video. That lets an agent read screenshots, charts, scanned pages, voice memos and meeting recordings without a separate model. It also operates desktop apps from screenshots. The 1M-token context window fits a full codebase or document set in one call. Output runs up to 512K tokens, 4x the 128K cap on both rivals. How does Muse Ember perform on benchmarks? All results below are at max reasoning effort, as reported by Meta. Some come from Artificial Analysis (AA), others from Meta’s internal suite. Agents : On AutomationBench-AA , 657 Zapier business workflows, Ember completes 37.8% of tasks. GPT-6 Luna reaches 20.2% and Claude Haiku 5.5 reaches 13.9%. On Agents’ Last Exam (internal), Ember scores 61.6 versus 57.1 and 57.0. Coding : Ember leads Terminal-Bench 4.0 with 40.9 versus Haiku’s 39.2 and Luna’s 16.4. It also leads the AA Coding Agent Index, 46 to 37 to 31. It loses FrontierCode 2.0-AA, where Haiku scores 34.9 and Ember 27.2. Multimodal : Ember ties GPT-6 Luna on GDP.pdf-AA at 22.8. It edges Haiku on OSWorld 2.1, 69.5 versus 68.9 on partial credit. PerceptionBench with tools gives Ember 80.6, Haiku 78.6 and Luna 62.8. Why is Muse Ember cheaper per task if token prices match? Muse Ember costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens . Cached input costs $0.004 per million. Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna list the same base rates. With identical list prices, the cost gap must come from tokens used per task. On Meta’s chart, Ember at max scores 35.8 for $0.136 per task. Haiku 5.5 at max scores 36.2 for $0.411. Luna’s best setting scores 27.8 for $0.152. Artificial Analysis summarised this as matching Haiku at a third of the cost per task. Long prompts widen the gap on paper. Haiku 5.5 charges $0.50 and $2.50 above 100K prompt tokens. GPT-6 Luna doubles input rates above 272K input tokens. Meta lists no long-context tier for Ember. articles.title: Why Eden Needed the Forbidden Fruit: A Lesson in Love and Free Will
articles.content: From here, I borrow the language of my faith. I hope readers who do not share that faith will read it as an old thought experiment. I have wondered since childhood: if Eden was perfect, why was the forbidden fruit there? Why plant a tree in the middle of the garden only to forbid eating from it? Without the tree, there would have been no failure. Thinking about the super second brain led me to read this question differently. Imagine Eden without the tree. Adam cannot leave God there, because there is no way to leave. We do not call it love when a being who cannot leave stays beside someone. I read that tree as a door left open so that staying can be a choice. English key to the original diagram. A tree stands in the center; a door has been left open. The open way out makes remaining in the garden a choice. Figure 16. Because the tree is there, staying becomes a choice. In the language of Chapter 12, the forbidden fruit is friction. Only where there is friction does love become a choice. The ‘complete observation’ of Chapter 8 looks different here, too. Adam in Eden lived before a God who knew all of him. From the beginning, there was no switch for turning off being known. What remained open to him was one door through which he could leave. Here I receive the switch I set aside in Chapter 8 in another form. Even if I cannot choose whether to be known, I can choose where to stay while fully known. Rereading old words In the prologue, I wrote that I have also understood the life of faith as training in metacognition. Placed beside the words I have come to use while building the super second brain, it looks like this. I am not using this table to make a theological claim. I want to show how I organize my thoughts by moving between the languages of these two worlds. I would like you to notice the place of atonement. In Chapter 6, I said that self-esteem is needed to withstand accurate criticism from a second brain. The firmest ground for self-esteem I know comes from outside achievement. In a world where AI remembers more and judges better than I do, self-esteem built on achievement cannot hold. 100 percent is not a place to stay In the prologue, I pushed fidelity to 100 percent. Now I need to revise that number. 100 percent is not somewhere I can arrive and stay, because I keep changing. The birth of a child brings fears that did not exist yesterday. Greater authority brings unfamiliar temptations. Loving someone new opens rooms inside me I did not know were there. Great pain rearranges the order of my values. New relationships, new desires, new power, new pain. As long as I live in the world with a body, these keep arriving, and each arrival makes me a slightly different person. The self-model that was at 100 percent yesterday is at 98 percent this morning. So the SSOT is never finished. And the material with which to rewrite it—the new me, not yet recorded anywhere—arises only at the standpoint of lived presence. Only when I, with a body, undergo something is there something new to write. Eden is not a world where choice has disappeared. It is a world where, despite being able to choose otherwise, one chooses love.

articles.title: Robotic Car Charger Locks On With Suction
articles.content: Not only does [Mew463]’s robotic car charger take care of plugging in his vehicle for him, it has some really clever features that are great to see in action. We’ve seen a rover-platform-based robotic car charger before , but what’s different here is that [Mew463]’s robot isn’t particularly husky. It’s designed to be low-profile, snug right up against the vehicle during use, and park itself against the wall when not. As an added touch, one doesn’t even have to manually open the car’s charge port door. The robot uses API calls that — once it confirms the vehicle is parked and not in use — unlocks and opens the charge port remotely. People used to be able to pop the charge port with a plain old wireless replay attack , but an API is the better way to go about it. Four Mecanum wheel and LiDAR get the robot into more or less the right position, then fine-tuning happens with the help of an onboard camera and a ChARuco board pattern on the car just under the charging port. Once things are lined up just right, the charger moves forward to plug into the car. Here’s where [Mew463] had to get clever, because plugging in a car charger actually takes a decent amount of force, and the robot is not particularly heavy. The solution is two suction cups that anchor the robot to the car as a gear assembly pushes the charger home. We really like how the robot snugs right up, so while the car is charging there isn’t a big thing in the way. Disconnecting is the reverse of the process, and for the robot to park itself again it simply swivels the camera backward so it can see the marker on the wall without the whole robot having to turn around. It’s all very slick, and you can watch it in action in the video embedded below.

articles.title: A week after the Democrats’ blue wave, Trump’s biggest tech allies are still silent
articles.content: “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time.” That was Elon Musk’s sarcastic response on X to the blue wave in the 2026 midterm elections . Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time 🤷‍♂️ — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 4, 2026 But almost a week later, Musk remains one of the few prominent Silicon Valley figures who backed Trump and his Republican allies to have publicly acknowledged the Democrats’ sweeping victories. It’s no surprise that Musk spoke out, given his outspoken nature in general and his massive spending on Republican candidates. The sometimes trillionaire CEO of Tesla and SpaceX spent about $474 million on the midterms , a record amount, and roughly $300 million more than the next-biggest donors, Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein, according to The New York Times . Yet Musk walked away from the November 3 election with little to show for his money, especially in his adopted home state of Texas, where nearly half of his nationwide donations had gone toward losing Republican candidates. As results poured in, Musk deleted his “Vote red today!” post on X, replacing it with “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.” A generally muted response While many of Trump’s Silicon Valley allies have remained quiet about the Democrats’ victories, some tech executives have addressed what the results could mean for their businesses—particularly the AI infrastructure boom. OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar said the company would continue investing in AI data centers, even after voters rejected local measures supporting their construction in 40 out of 41 instances, CNBC reports . “When I think about the midterms, I need to keep thinking about how do we keep investing to meet that customer demand,” Friar said on November 6. “It starts early with having built relationships with all of the hyperscalers, and it will continue to mean that we raise capital.” The day before, OpenAI announced a new commitment to pay for its own data centers, protect local resources, issue impact reports, and create local economic opportunities. The company billed the initiative, seemingly designed to ease concerns among communities and policymakers wary of AI infrastructure, as “Setting a new standard for responsible AI infrastructure.” Meanwhile, Box CEO Aaron Levie told CNBC the results could raise questions about where data centers get built and how AI supply chains operate. But on the broader political implications of the election, many of Trump’s Big Tech allies have remained mum. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang —all past Trump donors —have yet to comment publicly on the results. The silence marks a change from 2024 When Trump won the 2024 presidential election, many of those same tech leaders were quick to offer congratulations, often on Musk’s X. “Congrats to President Trump,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman posted at the time. “I wish for his huge success in the job. It is critically important that the US maintains its lead in developing AI with democratic values.” Pichai wrote , “Congratulations to President @realDonaldTrump on his decisive victory. We are in a golden age of American innovation and are committed to working with his administration to help bring the benefits to everyone.” Apple’s then-CEO Tim Cook echoed that sentiment : “Congratulations President Trump on your victory! We look forward to engaging with you and your administration to help make sure the United States continues to lead with and be fueled by ingenuity, innovation, and creativity.” “Congratulations to President Trump on a decisive victory,” Zuckerberg wrote on Meta’s Threads. “We have great opportunities ahead of us as a country. Looking forward to working with you and your administration.” Some Silicon Valley leaders welcomed the results Not everyone in Silicon Valley has been so quiet. While the tech industry has shifted sharply to the right in recent years,…
articles.author: Sarah Fielding

articles.title: MIT-led team receives funding to develop next-generation alternatives to modern weed killers
articles.content: MIT researchers will lead an up to $53 million effort, awarded by the U.S. Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health (ARPA-H) as part of its STREAM (Systems for Tracking and Resilience in Efficient Agricultural-input Management) program, to develop next-generation weed killers that help farmers and protect human health. More than 1 billion pounds of herbicide are used in the United States every year. Herbicides help farmers by preventing significant crop loss due to weeds, and they enable regenerative farming practices that protect the soil, but some weeds are becoming resistant to the most common herbicides. Exposure to herbicides may contribute to increased risk of cancer, metabolic and endocrine disorders, and other adverse health outcomes. Farm workers can be exposed from frequent herbicide use, but many U.S. residents are also exposed to these chemicals in small amounts through food and drinking water. The MIT-led research team will develop new generative artificial intelligence tools to help them discover herbicide alternatives that are more effective and developed with human health in mind. Such alternatives could also help to reduce U.S. dependency on imported phosphorus, which is a critical ingredient in a major herbicide, glyphosate. “With herbicides like glyphosate and atrazine, there’s a real crisis because of resistance mutations that are coming,” says Christopher Voigt, head of MIT’s Department of Biological Engineering. “And if you combine the resistance mutations with issues around national security of the supply chain of the precursors to herbicides, we could find ourselves without these core agrochemicals that are absolutely essential for getting the high crop yields and economical prices that the United States now sees.” Voigt is the principal investigator for the project, known as Precision Learning for On-target Weed control (PLOW). The team is also expected to include researchers from the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, the University of Tennessee at Knoxville, the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, and Robigo. The researchers are grouped into three teams that will tackle different aspects of the project, aligned with the STREAM Technical Areas. The generative AI group will develop models that can predict molecules — either chemical compounds or small interfering RNA (siRNA) — that disrupt the same plant enzymes targeted by glyphosate and other herbicides. Glyphosate kills weeds by interfering with an enzyme called EPSP synthase, which plants need to produce several critical amino acids. After many years of herbicide use, some weeds have begun to acquire genetic mutations that allow them to become resistant to those herbicides, which makes them less effective and poses a significant threat to crop yields. “There’s a real need for new herbicides because of resistance mutations that have been arising,” Voigt says. “There are also concerns about herbicides’ possible impacts on the environment and on humans, so it’s important to identify alternative ways of making herbicides, which as a general class of molecule are really critical to agriculture.” The MIT-led team plans to design generative AI models that will be able to predict molecules that can help prevent resistance from arising. The models will also optimize for other features such as low cost of synthesis, low risk of inducing resistance, and low risk of harming humans or causing ecological damage. The group developing these AI models is led by Connor Coley, the Warren K. Lewis Associate Professor of Chemical Engineering at MIT; Regina Barzilay, the School of Engineering Distinguished Professor for AI and Health at MIT; and Alexander Tropsha, the K.H. Lee Distinguished Professor in the UNC Eshelman School of Pharmacy. The models are expected to generate billions of possible candidates, which will then be tested by a second research team. This high-throughput screening group will be led…
